## Details
**1. MIMIC-CXR**: https://physionet.org/content/mimic-cxr/2.1.0/
- **Contents:** images from Beth Israel Deaconess in Boston, each study with its full report (findings and impression sections). It is the main benchmark in this field.
- **Access:** create a PhysioNet account → apply for credentialing (ID check and a reference) → complete the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" course → sign the agreement on the project page.
- **Agreement terms** (quoted on the page): no sharing, no attempt to re-identify, and "any publication which makes use of the data will also make the relevant code available."
- **Images:** MIMIC-CXR-JPG has JPGs and labels but no reports. Most papers use its images with the MIMIC-CXR reports; the same credential covers both.
- **Watch out:** PhysioNet's rules forbid sending this data to third-party online LLM services, so use local models or an approved cloud setup. Reports often refer to earlier exams; CXR-PRO on PhysioNet is a cleaned version with those references removed.
- **Paper using it:** "Evaluating progress in automatic chest X-ray radiology report generation" (Patterns 2023, [10.1016/j.patter.2023.100802](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patter.2023.100802)), which introduced the RadGraph F1 and RadCliQ metrics.

**2. CheXpert Plus**: https://aimi.stanford.edu/datasets/chexpert-plus
- **Contents:** Stanford Hospital reports, each split into 11 sections, with images as DICOM and PNG.
- **Access:** follow "Download here" to Redivis, log in, accept the agreement, then download the `df_chexpert_plus` CSV (the reports) and the images.
- **Terms:** search results quoting the agreement say research use only, no commercial use, no redistribution. I couldn't confirm whether Redivis approves requests automatically or by hand.
- **Why use it:** it is a second large English hospital, which makes it a good check of how well a MIMIC-trained model transfers.

**3. ReXGradient-160K**: https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGradient-160K
- **Contents:** reports with Indication, Comparison, Findings and Impression sections. Official train/validation/test splits are 140k/10k/10k, and a further 10k private test set backs the ReXrank leaderboard.
- **Access:** log in to Hugging Face and accept the agreement; this is the fastest way to get large-scale English data.
- **Limits:** non-commercial and non-clinical use only, no redistribution. Images are PNGs shrunk to 25% of original size.

**4. IU X-ray / Open-i** (openi.nlm.nih.gov)
- **Contents:** findings and impression text with frontal and lateral images. You can start on it today; it's commonly used as a second test set.
- **Check:** the site is a JavaScript app the tool couldn't read, so the download link and the CC BY-NC-ND licence are from memory. Confirm them in a browser and use the NLM original rather than Hugging Face copies.

**5–6. PadChest and PadChest-GR** (BIMCV, Spain): bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest/ and /padchest-gr/
- **PadChest:** Spanish reports from Hospital San Juan, about 1 TB. **Caveat:** the released report text was heavily normalised for anonymisation (case, accents and stop-words removed), so it isn't natural prose.
- **PadChest-GR:** reports written by radiologists in both Spanish and English, with a box for each finding. It is the cleanest bilingual option ([NEJM AI 2025](https://doi.org/10.1056/aidbp2401120)), but the reports were curated for the dataset rather than taken from clinical practice.
- **Access:** the BIMCV site returned errors (HTTP 503) today, so the request-form process comes from secondary sources ([arXiv 1901.07441](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.07441), [authors' GitHub](https://github.com/auriml/Rx-thorax-automatic-captioning)).

**7. CASIA-CXR (French)**: https://www.casia-cxr.net/
- **Contents:** narrative reports "originally written in French" ([Neurocomputing 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2024.128478)).
- **Access:** an ~80 MB sample is downloadable now; the full set needs a request form and a use agreement.
- **Unknowns:** the site gives no total size and names no licence.

**8. REFLACX**: https://physionet.org/content/reflacx-xray-localization/1.0.0/
- Reports dictated by radiologists while their eye movements were tracked, on MIMIC-CXR images. Useful as a supplement, not on its own.

**9. BIMCV-COVID19+**: Spanish reports, COVID-positive patients only, available by request under BIMCV's research use agreement. Its population is narrow.

**10. Naija-CXR**: https://zenodo.org/records/21781842

- The record says CC BY 4.0, but its description limits use to non-commercial research, so treat it as non-commercial.

- **Check:** the site is a JavaScript app the tool couldn't read, so the download link and the CC BY-NC-ND licence are from memory. Confirm them in a browser and use the NLM original rather than Hugging Face copies.

**5–6. PadChest and PadChest-GR** (BIMCV, Spain): bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest/ and /padchest-gr/
- **PadChest:** Spanish reports from Hospital San Juan, about 1 TB. **Caveat:** the released report text was heavily normalised for anonymisation (case, accents and stop-words removed), so it isn't natural prose.

- **Contents:** narrative reports "originally written in French" ([Neurocomputing 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2024.128478)).

- Reports dictated by radiologists while their eye movements were tracked, on MIMIC-CXR images. Useful as a supplement, not on its own.

**9. BIMCV-COVID19+**: Spanish reports, COVID-positive patients only, available by request under BIMCV's research use agreement. Its population is narrow.

**10. Naija-CXR**: https://zenodo.org/records/21781842
- A new (2026) Nigerian dataset whose contents list "free radiologist reports." Report coverage and image count aren't stated.
- The record says CC BY 4.0, but its description limits use to non-commercial research, so treat it as non-commercial.

## Details

**1. MIMIC-CXR** — https://physionet.org/content/mimic-cxr/2.1.0/
- **What's in it:** one full free-text report per study (Beth Israel Deaconess, Boston), with DICOM images. It's the default benchmark, so you'll need it for comparisons with published work (R2Gen, MAIRA-2 and similar).
- **Access, confirmed today:**
  1. Create a PhysioNet account.
  2. Complete the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" course.
  3. Apply for credentialing, which needs a reference.
  4. Sign the data use agreement. The page says: *"Only credentialed users who sign the DUA can access the files."*
- **Agreement terms:** no sharing the data, no attempts to re-identify anyone, and any publication must release its code.
- **Images:** for JPGs, use MIMIC-CXR-JPG (same credential). It has images and labels but no reports.
- **Limits:**
  - Access is personal: every team member must be credentialed.
  - Under PhysioNet's [LLM policy](https://physionet.org/news/post/llm-responsible-use/) you can't send the reports to a hosted LLM API unless zero data retention, no training on the data and no human review are verified.
  - Don't use the copies on Hugging Face (e.g. `X-iZhang/MIMIC-CXR-RRG`). They're unofficial, and the DUA still applies to them.

**2. ReXGradient-160K** — https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGradient-160K
- **What's in it, confirmed today:** reports from 3 US health systems (79 sites), *"unaltered except for PHI removal"*. They're split into Indication, Comparison, Findings and Impression.
  - Splits: 140k train, 10k validation, 10k public test. Another 10k studies are held back as a private test set for the ReXrank leaderboard.
- **Access:** log in to Hugging Face and accept the Non-Commercial Data Access and Use Agreement.
- **Limits:**
  - Use is non-commercial and non-clinical only.
  - Images are downsampled to 25% of their original size.
  - The report sections were split out with GPT-4o.

**3. CheXpert Plus** — https://aimi.stanford.edu/datasets/chexpert-plus
- **What's in it:** *"187,711 radiology reports, each meticulously divided into 11 subsections"*, aligned with the CheXpert images (Stanford Hospital). Code is at [github.com/Stanford-AIMI/chexpert-plus](https://github.com/Stanford-AIMI/chexpert-plus).
- **Access:** the AIMI page's "Download here" link goes to Redivis.
- **Not confirmed:** the licence name (Stanford University Dataset Research Use Agreement) comes from search results, not the page itself. I couldn't read the terms page because it's built with JavaScript. Check whether approval is manual and what it says about commercial use.

**4. IU X-ray / Open-i** — https://openi.nlm.nih.gov/faq
- `NLMCXR_png.tgz` and `NLMCXR_reports.tgz` under `openi.nlm.nih.gov/imgs/collections/` both responded today.
- The reports are XML with findings and impression. The "XXXX" strings are de-identification masks.
- It's too small to train on, so use it for prototyping and as a cross-institution test set.
- The CC BY-NC-ND licence is what the Academic Torrents mirror states; I didn't confirm it on Open-i.

**5. PadChest** — https://bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest/
- **What's in it:** Spanish reports from Hospital San Juan, Alicante, 2009–2017. About 1 TB, in 54 zip files.
- **Access:** a formal request through the site. You agree not to share the data and not to re-identify anyone (from the authors' GitHub). The site returned 503 errors today, so I couldn't confirm the current form.
- **Caveat for generation:** the released report text has been normalised: lower-cased, with stop words and word endings stripped. It isn't raw prose.

**6. PadChest-GR** — https://bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest-gr/ ([NEJM AI 2025](https://doi.org/10.1056/aidbp2401120))
- Built for grounded report generation: finding sentences (present and absent) in both English and Spanish, each with a bounding box.
- Available on request.
- Good for a bilingual secondary experiment.

**7. CASIA-CXR** — https://www.casia-cxr.net/ ([Neurocomputing 2024](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1016/j.neucom.2024.128478))
- **What's in it:** reports *"originally written in French"* with high-resolution frontal JPEGs from several French hospitals.
- **Access:** an ~80 MB sample is downloadable. For the full records the site says *"We may provide them upon request."*
- **Not confirmed:** no licence is stated on the pages I could read. The Hugging Face copy (FrancophonIA/CASIA-CXR) is empty.

**8. BIMCV-COVID19+** ([arXiv 2006.01174](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.01174))
- Spanish reports for COVID-19-positive patients from 11 hospitals in the Valencia region, available on request through BIMCV.
- The population is narrow, and it mixes CXR with CT, so you'd filter to the X-ray studies.

## Not recommended, and why
- **CANDID-PTX:** it does have 19k free-text reports, but the figshare record says today: *"not available for access by users outside Health New Zealand"* (closed since February 2024).
- **CheXpert (original), NIH ChestX-ray14, VinDr-CXR:** labels only, no report text. CheXpert's reports are what CheXpert Plus adds.
- **PARROT:** multilingual, but the reports are fictional and there are no images.

## What I could not find
- No public chest X-ray dataset with images and reports in Chinese, German, Portuguese or Vietnamese turned up.
- I couldn't confirm the current request forms or licences for the BIMCV datasets (PadChest, PadChest-GR, BIMCV-COVID19+) because the site was down. Retry it before you plan around them.

## Next step
1. Today: start MIMIC-CXR credentialing (the CITI course takes a few hours), accept the ReXGradient agreement, and download IU X-ray.
2. For the secondary experiment, PadChest-GR is the simplest choice: one study set with reports in both languages. If you'd rather have full-length non-English report text, use CASIA-CXR (French), since PadChest's released Spanish reports are preprocessed.
3. Check with your institution whether this work needs an ethics review exemption.

## Details

**1. MIMIC-CXR** — https://physionet.org/content/mimic-cxr/2.1.0/
- **What's in it:** one full free-text report per study (Beth Israel Deaconess, Boston), with DICOM images. It's the default benchmark, so you'll need it for comparisons with published work (R2Gen, MAIRA-2 and similar).
- **Access, confirmed today:**
  1. Create a PhysioNet account.
  2. Complete the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" course.
  3. Apply for credentialing, which needs a reference.
  4. Sign the data use agreement. The page says: *"Only credentialed users who sign the DUA can access the files."*
- **Agreement terms:** no sharing the data, no attempts to re-identify anyone, and any publication must release its code.
- **Images:** for JPGs, use MIMIC-CXR-JPG (same credential). It has images and labels but no reports.
- **Limits:**
  - Access is personal: every team member must be credentialed.
  - Under PhysioNet's [LLM policy](https://physionet.org/news/post/llm-responsible-use/) you can't send the reports to a hosted LLM API unless zero data retention, no training on the data and no human review are verified.
  - Don't use the copies on Hugging Face (e.g. `X-iZhang/MIMIC-CXR-RRG`). They're unofficial, and the DUA still applies to them.

**2. ReXGradient-160K** — https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGradient-160K
- **What's in it, confirmed today:** reports from 3 US health systems (79 sites), *"unaltered except for PHI removal"*. They're split into Indication, Comparison, Findings and Impression.
  - Splits: 140k train, 10k validation, 10k public test. Another 10k studies are held back as a private test set for the ReXrank leaderboard.
- **Access:** log in to Hugging Face and accept the Non-Commercial Data Access and Use Agreement.
- **Limits:**
  - Use is non-commercial and non-clinical only.
  - Images are downsampled to 25% of their original size.
  - The report sections were split out with GPT-4o.

**3. CheXpert Plus** — https://aimi.stanford.edu/datasets/chexpert-plus
- **What's in it:** *"187,711 radiology reports, each meticulously divided into 11 subsections"*, aligned with the CheXpert images (Stanford Hospital). Code is at [github.com/Stanford-AIMI/chexpert-plus](https://github.com/Stanford-AIMI/chexpert-plus).
- **Access:** the AIMI page's "Download here" link goes to Redivis.
- **Not confirmed:** the licence name (Stanford University Dataset Research Use Agreement) comes from search results, not the page itself. I couldn't read the terms page because it's built with JavaScript. Check whether approval is manual and what it says about commercial use.

**4. IU X-ray / Open-i** — https://openi.nlm.nih.gov/faq
- `NLMCXR_png.tgz` and `NLMCXR_reports.tgz` under `openi.nlm.nih.gov/imgs/collections/` both responded today.
- The reports are XML with findings and impression. The "XXXX" strings are de-identification masks.
- It's too small to train on, so use it for prototyping and as a cross-institution test set.
- The CC BY-NC-ND licence is what the Academic Torrents mirror states; I didn't confirm it on Open-i.

**5. PadChest** — https://bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest/
- **What's in it:** Spanish reports from Hospital San Juan, Alicante, 2009–2017. About 1 TB, in 54 zip files.
- **Access:** a formal request through the site. You agree not to share the data and not to re-identify anyone (from the authors' GitHub). The site returned 503 errors today, so I couldn't confirm the current form.
- **Caveat for generation:** the released report text has been normalised: lower-cased, with stop words and word endings stripped. It isn't raw prose.

**6. PadChest-GR** — https://bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest-gr/ ([NEJM AI 2025](https://doi.org/10.1056/aidbp2401120))
- Built for grounded report generation: finding sentences (present and absent) in both English and Spanish, each with a bounding box.
- Available on request.
- Good for a bilingual secondary experiment.

**7. CASIA-CXR** — https://www.casia-cxr.net/ ([Neurocomputing 2024](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1016/j.neucom.2024.128478))
- **What's in it:** reports *"originally written in French"* with high-resolution frontal JPEGs from several French hospitals.
- **Access:** an ~80 MB sample is downloadable. For the full records the site says *"We may provide them upon request."*
- **Not confirmed:** no licence is stated on the pages I could read. The Hugging Face copy (FrancophonIA/CASIA-CXR) is empty.

**8. BIMCV-COVID19+** ([arXiv 2006.01174](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.01174))
- Spanish reports for COVID-19-positive patients from 11 hospitals in the Valencia region, available on request through BIMCV.
- The population is narrow, and it mixes CXR with CT, so you'd filter to the X-ray studies.

## Not recommended, and why
- **CANDID-PTX:** it does have 19k free-text reports, but the figshare record says today: *"not available for access by users outside Health New Zealand"* (closed since February 2024).
- **CheXpert (original), NIH ChestX-ray14, VinDr-CXR:** labels only, no report text. CheXpert's reports are what CheXpert Plus adds.
- **PARROT:** multilingual, but the reports are fictional and there are no images.

## What I could not find
- No public chest X-ray dataset with images and reports in Chinese, German, Portuguese or Vietnamese turned up.
- I couldn't confirm the current request forms or licences for the BIMCV datasets (PadChest, PadChest-GR, BIMCV-COVID19+) because the site was down. Retry it before you plan around them.

## Next step
1. Today: start MIMIC-CXR credentialing (the CITI course takes a few hours), accept the ReXGradient agreement, and download IU X-ray.
2. For the secondary experiment, PadChest-GR is the simplest choice: one study set with reports in both languages. If you'd rather have full-length non-English report text, use CASIA-CXR (French), since PadChest's released Spanish reports are preprocessed.
3. Check with your institution whether this work needs an ethics review exemption.

The interactive page with filters and an access-plan export is at `/private/tmp/e-tg8IBR/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

## Details

**1. MIMIC-CXR** — https://physionet.org/content/mimic-cxr/2.1.0/
- **What's in it:** one full free-text report per study (Beth Israel Deaconess, Boston), with DICOM images. It's the default benchmark, so you'll need it for comparisons with published work (R2Gen, MAIRA-2 and similar).
- **Access, confirmed today:**
  1. Create a PhysioNet account.
  2. Complete the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" course.
  3. Apply for credentialing, which needs a reference.
  4. Sign the data use agreement. The page says: *"Only credentialed users who sign the DUA can access the files."*
- **Agreement terms:** no sharing the data, no attempts to re-identify anyone, and any publication must release its code.
- **Images:** for JPGs, use MIMIC-CXR-JPG (same credential). It has images and labels but no reports.
- **Limits:**
  - Access is personal: every team member must be credentialed.
  - Under PhysioNet's [LLM policy](https://physionet.org/news/post/llm-responsible-use/) you can't send the reports to a hosted LLM API unless zero data retention, no training on the data and no human review are verified.
  - Don't use the copies on Hugging Face (e.g. `X-iZhang/MIMIC-CXR-RRG`). They're unofficial, and the DUA still applies to them.

**2. ReXGradient-160K** — https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGradient-160K
- **What's in it, confirmed today:** reports from 3 US health systems (79 sites), *"unaltered except for PHI removal"*. They're split into Indication, Comparison, Findings and Impression.
  - Splits: 140k train, 10k validation, 10k public test. Another 10k studies are held back as a private test set for the ReXrank leaderboard.
- **Access:** log in to Hugging Face and accept the Non-Commercial Data Access and Use Agreement.
- **Limits:**
  - Use is non-commercial and non-clinical only.
  - Images are downsampled to 25% of their original size.
  - The report sections were split out with GPT-4o.

**3. CheXpert Plus** — https://aimi.stanford.edu/datasets/chexpert-plus
- **What's in it:** *"187,711 radiology reports, each meticulously divided into 11 subsections"*, aligned with the CheXpert images (Stanford Hospital). Code is at [github.com/Stanford-AIMI/chexpert-plus](https://github.com/Stanford-AIMI/chexpert-plus).
- **Access:** the AIMI page's "Download here" link goes to Redivis.
- **Not confirmed:** the licence name (Stanford University Dataset Research Use Agreement) comes from search results, not the page itself. I couldn't read the terms page because it's built with JavaScript. Check whether approval is manual and what it says about commercial use.

**4. IU X-ray / Open-i** — https://openi.nlm.nih.gov/faq
- `NLMCXR_png.tgz` and `NLMCXR_reports.tgz` under `openi.nlm.nih.gov/imgs/collections/` both responded today.
- The reports are XML with findings and impression. The "XXXX" strings are de-identification masks.
- It's too small to train on, so use it for prototyping and as a cross-institution test set.
- The CC BY-NC-ND licence is what the Academic Torrents mirror states; I didn't confirm it on Open-i.

**5. PadChest** — https://bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest/
- **What's in it:** Spanish reports from Hospital San Juan, Alicante, 2009–2017. About 1 TB, in 54 zip files.
- **Access:** a formal request through the site. You agree not to share the data and not to re-identify anyone (from the authors' GitHub). The site returned 503 errors today, so I couldn't confirm the current form.
- **Caveat for generation:** the released report text has been normalised: lower-cased, with stop words and word endings stripped. It isn't raw prose.

**6. PadChest-GR** — https://bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest-gr/ ([NEJM AI 2025](https://doi.org/10.1056/aidbp2401120))
- Built for grounded report generation: finding sentences (present and absent) in both English and Spanish, each with a bounding box.
- Available on request.
- Good for a bilingual secondary experiment.

**7. CASIA-CXR** — https://www.casia-cxr.net/ ([Neurocomputing 2024](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1016/j.neucom.2024.128478))
- **What's in it:** reports *"originally written in French"* with high-resolution frontal JPEGs from several French hospitals.
- **Access:** an ~80 MB sample is downloadable. For the full records the site says *"We may provide them upon request."*
- **Not confirmed:** no licence is stated on the pages I could read. The Hugging Face copy (FrancophonIA/CASIA-CXR) is empty.

**8. BIMCV-COVID19+** ([arXiv 2006.01174](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.01174))
- Spanish reports for COVID-19-positive patients from 11 hospitals in the Valencia region, available on request through BIMCV.
- The population is narrow, and it mixes CXR with CT, so you'd filter to the X-ray studies.

## Not recommended, and why
- **CANDID-PTX:** it does have 19k free-text reports, but the figshare record says today: *"not available for access by users outside Health New Zealand"* (closed since February 2024).
- **CheXpert (original), NIH ChestX-ray14, VinDr-CXR:** labels only, no report text. CheXpert's reports are what CheXpert Plus adds.
- **PARROT:** multilingual, but the reports are fictional and there are no images.

## What I could not find
- No public chest X-ray dataset with images and reports in Chinese, German, Portuguese or Vietnamese turned up.
- I couldn't confirm the current request forms or licences for the BIMCV datasets (PadChest, PadChest-GR, BIMCV-COVID19+) because the site was down. Retry it before you plan around them.

2. For the secondary experiment, PadChest-GR is the simplest choice: one study set with reports in both languages. If you'd rather have full-length non-English report text, use CASIA-CXR (French), since PadChest's released Spanish reports are preprocessed.

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
The datasets below pair images with the radiologist's actual report text. I wrote this from memory and didn't look anything up for this answer, so check sizes, licences and access steps on each dataset's page before you rely on them.

## English free-text reports

| Dataset | Scale | Source | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MIMIC-CXR** (PhysioNet) | ~377K images, ~228K studies, ~65K patients | Beth Israel Deaconess (Boston), ER/inpatient | Credentialed |
| **CheXpert Plus** (Stanford AIMI, 2024) | ~223K image–report pairs, ~65K patients | Stanford Hospital | Research-use agreement |
| **ReXGradient-160K** (2025) | ~160K studies, ~109K patients | 3 US health systems, ~79 sites | Gated Hugging Face |
| **IU X-Ray / Open-i** | ~7.5K images, ~3.9K reports | Indiana University | Open download |
| **CANDID-PTX** | ~19K images with reports | Dunedin, New Zealand (focus on pneumothorax) | DUA with Univ. of Otago |

**MIMIC-CXR**
- **Getting it:** create a PhysioNet account, get credentialed (identity check plus a reference), finish the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" course, then sign the DUA for the dataset. This usually takes a few days to a couple of weeks.
- **Images vs. reports:** the reports are in `mimic-cxr-reports.zip` in the main MIMIC-CXR project, which also holds the DICOMs (~4.7 TB). Most people use **MIMIC-CXR-JPG** (~570 GB) for the images. It also has the standard train/val/test split and CheXpert labels, but no report text. So you sign two DUAs and join the two on study ID.
- **LLM restriction:** PhysioNet's rules don't allow sending the data to third-party chat services like the consumer ChatGPT site. Hosted APIs with no data retention (e.g. Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex) are allowed under their responsible-use guidance. This matters if you plan to use LLMs for preprocessing or evaluation.
- **Standing:** it's the de facto benchmark, so you'll need it for comparisons with published work.

**CheXpert Plus**
- The original CheXpert only shipped labels. Plus adds the de-identified reports, parsed into sections, along with RadGraph annotations and demographics.
- **Getting it:** register on Stanford AIMI, accept the Stanford research-use agreement, then download from Azure. It's large; DICOM and PNG versions are both offered.

**ReXGradient-160K**
- **Getting it:** accept the terms on the gated Hugging Face repo (from the Rajpurkar lab).
- It ships train/val/public-test splits plus a held-out private test set.
- Because the images come from many sites, it's useful for testing generalization beyond a single hospital.

**IU X-Ray (Open-i)**
- **Getting it:** no credentialing; download directly from NLM's Open-i. It's licensed for non-commercial use, so check the exact terms.
- Reports come as XML with Findings and Impression sections. De-identification replaced some content with "XXXX".
- It's small and has no official split, so papers' numbers aren't directly comparable. Use it for quick prototyping or as a second test set.

**CANDID-PTX**
- **Getting it:** a data use agreement plus proof of human-subjects training.
- It's skewed toward pneumothorax, chest tubes and rib fractures, so it's better as an extra evaluation set than as general training data.

## Non-English (for your secondary experiment)

- **PadChest** (Spain, BIMCV/Alicante): ~160K images and ~110K studies with **Spanish** reports. I believe the report text is somewhat preprocessed rather than fully raw, so look at a sample before committing. **Getting it:** fill out the BIMCV request form; it's free for research. About 1 TB.
- **PadChest-GR** (2024–25): a few thousand PadChest studies with grounded report sentences in **both Spanish and English**, plus bounding boxes. **Getting it:** through BIMCV under an agreement. It works well for a cross-lingual or grounded-generation experiment.
- **BIMCV-COVID19+** (Spain): I think it includes some Spanish reports, but I'm not certain. Check before relying on it.

## Common datasets that don't have report text
NIH ChestX-ray14, the original CheXpert, VinDr-CXR, and BRAX (as far as I know) only release labels or annotations. Datasets built on top of MIMIC-CXR, such as Chest ImaGenome, MS-CXR and RadGraph, add annotations but still need MIMIC-CXR access to get the reports.

## Practical notes
- **Which section to generate:** most papers generate the **Findings** section, sometimes Impression, so decide this early. A sizeable share of MIMIC studies have no Findings section.
- **References to prior exams:** reports often say things like "unchanged from prior". Consider CXR-PRO (MIMIC with those references removed) or using the prior study as an input.
- **Suggested plan:** start with IU X-Ray (instant download) while the MIMIC-CXR credentialing goes through. Then use MIMIC-CXR as the main benchmark, with CheXpert Plus and ReXGradient for training scale and testing on other hospitals' data.

- **Images vs. reports:** the reports are in `mimic-cxr-reports.zip` in the main MIMIC-CXR project, which also holds the DICOMs (~4.7 TB). Most people use **MIMIC-CXR-JPG** (~570 GB) for the images. It also has the standard train/val/test split and CheXpert labels, but no report text. So you sign two DUAs and join the two on study ID.
- **LLM restriction:** PhysioNet's rules don't allow sending the data to third-party chat services like the consumer ChatGPT site. Hosted APIs with no data retention (e.g. Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex) are allowed under their responsible-use guidance. This matters if you plan to use LLMs for preprocessing or evaluation.
- **Standing:** it's the de facto benchmark, so you'll need it for comparisons with published work.

**CheXpert Plus**
- The original CheXpert only shipped labels. Plus adds the de-identified reports, parsed into sections, along with RadGraph annotations and demographics.
- **Getting it:** register on Stanford AIMI, accept the Stanford research-use agreement, then download from Azure. It's large; DICOM and PNG versions are both offered.

**ReXGradient-160K**
- **Getting it:** accept the terms on the gated Hugging Face repo (from the Rajpurkar lab).
- It ships train/val/public-test splits plus a held-out private test set.
- Because the images come from many sites, it's useful for testing generalization beyond a single hospital.

**IU X-Ray (Open-i)**
- **Getting it:** no credentialing; download directly from NLM's Open-i. It's licensed for non-commercial use, so check the exact terms.
- Reports come as XML with Findings and Impression sections. De-identification replaced some content with "XXXX".
- It's small and has no official split, so papers' numbers aren't directly comparable. Use it for quick prototyping or as a second test set.

**CANDID-PTX**
- **Getting it:** a data use agreement plus proof of human-subjects training.
- It's skewed toward pneumothorax, chest tubes and rib fractures, so it's better as an extra evaluation set than as general training data.

## Non-English (for your secondary experiment)

- **PadChest** (Spain, BIMCV/Alicante): ~160K images and ~110K studies with **Spanish** reports. I believe the report text is somewhat preprocessed rather than fully raw, so look at a sample before committing. **Getting it:** fill out the BIMCV request form; it's free for research. About 1 TB.
- **PadChest-GR** (2024–25): a few thousand PadChest studies with grounded report sentences in **both Spanish and English**, plus bounding boxes. **Getting it:** through BIMCV under an agreement. It works well for a cross-lingual or grounded-generation experiment.
- **BIMCV-COVID19+** (Spain): I think it includes some Spanish reports, but I'm not certain. Check before relying on it.

## Common datasets that don't have report text
NIH ChestX-ray14, the original CheXpert, VinDr-CXR, and BRAX (as far as I know) only release labels or annotations. Datasets built on top of MIMIC-CXR, such as Chest ImaGenome, MS-CXR and RadGraph, add annotations but still need MIMIC-CXR access to get the reports.

## Practical notes
- **Which section to generate:** most papers generate the **Findings** section, sometimes Impression, so decide this early. A sizeable share of MIMIC studies have no Findings section.
- **References to prior exams:** reports often say things like "unchanged from prior". Consider CXR-PRO (MIMIC with those references removed) or using the prior study as an input.
- **Suggested plan:** start with IU X-Ray (instant download) while the MIMIC-CXR credentialing goes through. Then use MIMIC-CXR as the main benchmark, with CheXpert Plus and ReXGradient for training scale and testing on other hospitals' data.

The datasets below pair images with the radiologist's actual report text. I wrote this from memory and didn't look anything up for this answer, so check sizes, licences and access steps on each dataset's page before you rely on them.

## English free-text reports

| Dataset | Scale | Source | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MIMIC-CXR** (PhysioNet) | ~377K images, ~228K studies, ~65K patients | Beth Israel Deaconess (Boston), ER/inpatient | Credentialed |
| **CheXpert Plus** (Stanford AIMI, 2024) | ~223K image–report pairs, ~65K patients | Stanford Hospital | Research-use agreement |
| **ReXGradient-160K** (2025) | ~160K studies, ~109K patients | 3 US health systems, ~79 sites | Gated Hugging Face |
| **IU X-Ray / Open-i** | ~7.5K images, ~3.9K reports | Indiana University | Open download |
| **CANDID-PTX** | ~19K images with reports | Dunedin, New Zealand (focus on pneumothorax) | DUA with Univ. of Otago |

**MIMIC-CXR**
- **Getting it:** create a PhysioNet account, get credentialed (identity check plus a reference), finish the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" course, then sign the DUA for the dataset. This usually takes a few days to a couple of weeks.
- **Images vs. reports:** the reports are in `mimic-cxr-reports.zip` in the main MIMIC-CXR project, which also holds the DICOMs (~4.7 TB). Most people use **MIMIC-CXR-JPG** (~570 GB) for the images. It also has the standard train/val/test split and CheXpert labels, but no report text. So you sign two DUAs and join the two on study ID.
- **LLM restriction:** PhysioNet's rules don't allow sending the data to third-party chat services like the consumer ChatGPT site. Hosted APIs with no data retention (e.g. Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex) are allowed under their responsible-use guidance. This matters if you plan to use LLMs for preprocessing or evaluation.
- **Standing:** it's the de facto benchmark, so you'll need it for comparisons with published work.

**CheXpert Plus**
- The original CheXpert only shipped labels. Plus adds the de-identified reports, parsed into sections, along with RadGraph annotations and demographics.
- **Getting it:** register on Stanford AIMI, accept the Stanford research-use agreement, then download from Azure. It's large; DICOM and PNG versions are both offered.

**ReXGradient-160K**
- **Getting it:** accept the terms on the gated Hugging Face repo (from the Rajpurkar lab).
- It ships train/val/public-test splits plus a held-out private test set.
- Because the images come from many sites, it's useful for testing generalization beyond a single hospital.

**IU X-Ray (Open-i)**
- **Getting it:** no credentialing; download directly from NLM's Open-i. It's licensed for non-commercial use, so check the exact terms.
- Reports come as XML with Findings and Impression sections. De-identification replaced some content with "XXXX".
- It's small and has no official split, so papers' numbers aren't directly comparable. Use it for quick prototyping or as a second test set.

**CANDID-PTX**
- **Getting it:** a data use agreement plus proof of human-subjects training.
- It's skewed toward pneumothorax, chest tubes and rib fractures, so it's better as an extra evaluation set than as general training data.

## Non-English (for your secondary experiment)

- **PadChest** (Spain, BIMCV/Alicante): ~160K images and ~110K studies with **Spanish** reports. I believe the report text is somewhat preprocessed rather than fully raw, so look at a sample before committing. **Getting it:** fill out the BIMCV request form; it's free for research. About 1 TB.
- **PadChest-GR** (2024–25): a few thousand PadChest studies with grounded report sentences in **both Spanish and English**, plus bounding boxes. **Getting it:** through BIMCV under an agreement. It works well for a cross-lingual or grounded-generation experiment.
- **BIMCV-COVID19+** (Spain): I think it includes some Spanish reports, but I'm not certain. Check before relying on it.

## Common datasets that don't have report text
NIH ChestX-ray14, the original CheXpert, VinDr-CXR, and BRAX (as far as I know) only release labels or annotations. Datasets built on top of MIMIC-CXR, such as Chest ImaGenome, MS-CXR and RadGraph, add annotations but still need MIMIC-CXR access to get the reports.

## Practical notes
- **Which section to generate:** most papers generate the **Findings** section, sometimes Impression, so decide this early. A sizeable share of MIMIC studies have no Findings section.
- **References to prior exams:** reports often say things like "unchanged from prior". Consider CXR-PRO (MIMIC with those references removed) or using the prior study as an input.
- **Suggested plan:** start with IU X-Ray (instant download) while the MIMIC-CXR credentialing goes through. Then use MIMIC-CXR as the main benchmark, with CheXpert Plus and ReXGradient for training scale and testing on other hospitals' data.

Here are the main chest X-ray datasets that include the actual report text, starting with the most useful. Numbers and access terms are from memory, not checked live, so confirm the current license and version on each dataset's page before you apply.

## English, with full report text

**1. MIMIC-CXR (PhysioNet, Beth Israel Deaconess, Boston)**: the standard benchmark
- **Size:** about 377K images, 228K studies, 65K patients. Each study has one de-identified report with FINDINGS and IMPRESSION sections.
- **Access:** you need a PhysioNet credentialed account (ID check plus a reference), the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" course, and a signed data use agreement. Approval usually takes days to a few weeks.
- **Files:** the reports come as `mimic-cxr-reports.zip` in the DICOM release. MIMIC-CXR-JPG (about 570 GB) is the practical image source. The full DICOM set is about 4.7 TB. Official train/validate/test splits exist.
- **Restrictions:** the agreement forbids sending the data to third-party APIs, including hosted LLMs, unless the deployment is compliant. That matters if you plan LLM-based evaluation or augmentation.
- **Extras:** derived datasets like Chest ImaGenome, MS-CXR (phrase grounding) and CXR-PRO (reports with prior-study references removed) use the same credentials.

**2. CheXpert Plus (Stanford AIMI, 2024)**
- **Size:** about 223K image–report pairs, 188K studies, 65K patients. Reports are split into sections (findings, impression, history and so on), with patient metadata and RadGraph annotations.
- **Access:** register on the Stanford AIMI shared datasets portal and accept the research use agreement. It's non-commercial only, and there's no credentialing step like PhysioNet's.
- **Files:** downloads are hosted on Azure. The full image set is several TB, so plan storage and bandwidth.
- **Note:** this is the only CheXpert release with report text; the original CheXpert has labels only.

**3. ReXGradient-160K (Harvard Rajpurkar lab and Gradient Health, 2025)**
- **Size:** about 160K studies from about 109K patients across many US sites, with findings and impression text. Its multi-site data is good for testing whether a model generalizes beyond one hospital.
- **Access:** gated download on Hugging Face (accept the terms). Part of the test set is held back for the ReXrank leaderboard. Check the card for current license and split details.

**4. IU X-Ray / Open-i (Indiana University, via NLM)**
- **Size:** about 3,955 reports and 7,470 frontal and lateral images. Small, but the report format is clean.
- **Access:** fully public. Download from NLM's Open-i site, or use Kaggle mirrors.
- **Caveats:** too small to train on alone, and commonly used as an external test set. De-identification replaced some words with "XXXX", which you'll need to handle. Many papers use their own splits, so results across papers aren't directly comparable.

**5. CANDID-PTX (Dunedin, New Zealand)**
- **Size:** about 19K radiographs with free-text reports, plus pneumothorax, rib fracture and chest tube labels. A useful non-US English source.
- **Access:** request through Figshare. You complete ethics or human-subjects training and sign a data use agreement.

## Non-English

**6. PadChest (Spanish; BIMCV, Hospital San Juan, Alicante)**: the best option for your secondary experiment
- **Size:** about 160K images, 110K studies, 67K patients, with a Spanish report field.
- **Caveat:** the released "report" is preprocessed (normalized, lowercased, lightly cleaned), not the radiologist's raw prose. Whether that's acceptable depends on your experiment.
- **Access:** fill in the request form on the BIMCV site. It's free for research. The download is about 1 TB.
- **PadChest-GR (2024–25):** a smaller (about 4.5K studies) companion with grounded findings sentences in both Spanish and English, plus bounding boxes. It's handy for bilingual or grounded report generation.

**7. BIMCV-COVID19+ (Spanish)**: COVID-era chest X-rays and CTs with Spanish reports, distributed through BIMCV. Narrower in what it covers, but real report text.

## Datasets that look relevant but have labels only
NIH ChestX-ray14, original CheXpert, VinDr-CXR and BRAX (Brazil) ship labels extracted from reports, not the reports themselves. ROCO, MedPix and similar sets have figure captions or teaching-case text, not clinical reports.

## Suggested plan
- **Main training:** MIMIC-CXR. Start the PhysioNet credentialing now, since it's the slowest step.
- **More training data and external tests:** CheXpert Plus and ReXGradient-160K, with IU X-Ray as a quick public sanity check you can run on day one.
- **Secondary experiment:** PadChest, or PadChest-GR if you want parallel English text.
- **Data agreements:** check each one's terms on cloud compute and LLM APIs before you build your evaluation pipeline. MIMIC's terms in particular affect GPT- or Claude-based scoring like GREEN.

**1. MIMIC-CXR (PhysioNet, Beth Israel Deaconess, Boston)**: the standard benchmark
- **Size:** about 377K images, 228K studies, 65K patients. Each study has one de-identified report with FINDINGS and IMPRESSION sections.
- **Access:** you need a PhysioNet credentialed account (ID check plus a reference), the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" course, and a signed data use agreement. Approval usually takes days to a few weeks.
- **Files:** the reports come as `mimic-cxr-reports.zip` in the DICOM release. MIMIC-CXR-JPG (about 570 GB) is the practical image source. The full DICOM set is about 4.7 TB. Official train/validate/test splits exist.
- **Restrictions:** the agreement forbids sending the data to third-party APIs, including hosted LLMs, unless the deployment is compliant. That matters if you plan LLM-based evaluation or augmentation.

**2. CheXpert Plus (Stanford AIMI, 2024)**
- **Size:** about 223K image–report pairs, 188K studies, 65K patients. Reports are split into sections (findings, impression, history and so on), with patient metadata and RadGraph annotations.

- **Files:** downloads are hosted on Azure. The full image set is several TB, so plan storage and bandwidth.

**3. ReXGradient-160K (Harvard Rajpurkar lab and Gradient Health, 2025)**
- **Size:** about 160K studies from about 109K patients across many US sites, with findings and impression text. Its multi-site data is good for testing whether a model generalizes beyond one hospital.
- **Access:** gated download on Hugging Face (accept the terms). Part of the test set is held back for the ReXrank leaderboard. Check the card for current license and split details.

**4. IU X-Ray / Open-i (Indiana University, via NLM)**
- **Size:** about 3,955 reports and 7,470 frontal and lateral images. Small, but the report format is clean.
- **Access:** fully public. Download from NLM's Open-i site, or use Kaggle mirrors.
- **Caveats:** too small to train on alone, and commonly used as an external test set. De-identification replaced some words with "XXXX", which you'll need to handle. Many papers use their own splits, so results across papers aren't directly comparable.

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
Five main public datasets pair chest X-rays with the radiologist's actual report text. Four are in English, and PadChest is the main non-English (Spanish) option. Most CXR datasets only release labels extracted from the reports, so the list is short.

## English free-text reports

**1. MIMIC-CXR (Beth Israel Deaconess, Boston)**
- **Size:** about 377K images, 227K studies and 65K patients, with full reports (findings, impression, indication, comparison).
- **Access:** through PhysioNet. You need a credentialed account (ID check plus a reference), the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" human-subjects course, and a signed data use agreement. Expect this to take a few days to a couple of weeks.
- **Files:** the reports are in the MIMIC-CXR DICOM release (`mimic-cxr-reports.zip`). Most people use MIMIC-CXR-JPG for images (about 570 GB) and take the reports from the main release. The full DICOM set is several TB.
- **Watch out:** the PhysioNet agreement forbids sending the data to third-party services. That includes consumer LLM APIs, which matters if you plan to use LLMs for evaluation or report cleanup. PhysioNet has published guidance on which hosted setups are acceptable.
- **Role:** the de facto standard benchmark for report generation, so you'll almost certainly need it for comparisons.

**2. CheXpert Plus (Stanford)**
- **Size:** 223K report–image pairs, 188K studies and 65K patients. Reports are split into sections, and the release includes DICOM and PNG images, demographics, CheXpert/CheXbert labels and RadGraph annotations.
- **Access:** register on the Stanford AIMI Shared Datasets site and accept a research-use agreement (non-commercial, no redistribution). It's quicker than PhysioNet because no training course is required.
- **Watch out:** the official test set is tiny (about 200 studies, and only about 61 have a Findings section), so plan your own splits.

**3. ReXGradient-160K (Gradient Health / Rajpurkar lab, 2025)**
- **Size:** 160K studies, about 273K images and about 109K patients from 79 US sites across several health systems. That makes it more diverse than single-hospital sets.
- **Format:** images are PNGs converted from DICOM. GPT-4o was used to split the reports into sections, so the text is sectioned but not raw.
- **Access:** a gated Hugging Face dataset (`rajpurkarlab/ReXGradient-160K`). You accept the license on the dataset page, which is the fastest route here.
- **Splits:** train/validation/public test of 140K/10K/10K, plus a private 10K test set behind the ReXrank leaderboard. A later paper gives slightly larger counts, probably because it includes the private split.

**4. IU X-ray / Open-i (Indiana University, via NLM)**
- **Size:** about 7.5K images and about 3.9K reports with findings and impression.
- **Access:** free download from Open-i with no agreement step.
- **Watch out:** it's small, and de-identification replaced many tokens with "XXXX". It's fine for prototyping and as a second benchmark, but too small to train on alone.

**5. CANDID-PTX (Dunedin, New Zealand)**
- **Size:** about 19K CXRs with free-text reports, focused on pneumothorax, chest tubes and rib fractures.
- **Access:** you need a data use agreement, and typically institutional ethics approval, so it's slower to get.
- **Role:** useful as an out-of-distribution English test set from a non-US site.

## Non-English

**PadChest (Hospital San Juan, Alicante): Spanish**
- **Size:** about 160K images, 67K patients and about 110K reports, with 174 labeled findings mapped to UMLS.
- **Access:** request it through a form on the BIMCV site, agreeing not to share the data or try to re-identify anyone.
- **Watch out:** the release contains report excerpts that were preprocessed, possibly normalized. Check that the text is close enough to the original reports for your generation experiment before you rely on it.
- **PadChest-GR:** a smaller derived set with 4,555 studies and finding-level sentences in both Spanish and English, plus bounding boxes. It's good for grounded or bilingual generation, and you request it through BIMCV too.

**BIMCV-COVID19+ (Valencia)** also includes Spanish reports, but it's narrower (COVID-era cohort).

## What to skip
These are often mistaken for report datasets but only release labels or derived annotations:
- **Label-only sets:** ChestX-ray14 (NIH), the original CheXpert, VinDr-CXR and BRAX.
- **MIMIC derivatives:** Chest ImaGenome, MS-CXR and CXR-PRO add annotations or cleaned reports to MIMIC. They need the same PhysioNet credentials and don't add any new patients.
- **Caption sets:** ROCO and MedPix have figure captions, not clinical reports.

## Suggested plan
1. Start the PhysioNet credentialing now, because it has the longest lead time.
2. Meanwhile, accept the ReXGradient license and register for CheXpert Plus, which are both quick.
3. Train on MIMIC-CXR and/or CheXpert Plus, and test across institutions on ReXGradient and IU X-ray.
4. Request PadChest or PadChest-GR for the Spanish experiment.

I checked the ReXGradient, CheXpert Plus and PadChest details against current sources. The MIMIC-CXR, IU X-ray, CANDID-PTX and BIMCV details are from my own knowledge, so confirm sizes and terms on their pages before you depend on them.

Sources:
- [ReXGradient-160K paper (arXiv 2505.00228)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00228)
- [ReXGradient-160K on Hugging Face (paper page)](https://huggingface.co/papers/2505.00228)
- [ReXVQA paper (alternate ReXGradient counts)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.04353)
- [CheXpert Plus paper (arXiv 2405.19538)](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.19538)
- [CheXpert Plus GitHub](https://github.com/Stanford-AIMI/chexpert-plus)
- [PadChest paper (arXiv 1901.07441)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.07441)
- [PadChest access notes (GitHub repo)](https://github.com/auriml/Rx-thorax-automatic-captioning)
- [PadChest-GR](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/385700830_PadChest-GR_A_Bilingual_Chest_X-ray_Dataset_for_Grounded_Radiology_Report_Generation)
- [Report generation review (arXiv 2405.10842)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.10842)

- **Watch out:** the PhysioNet agreement forbids sending the data to third-party services. That includes consumer LLM APIs, which matters if you plan to use LLMs for evaluation or report cleanup. PhysioNet has published guidance on which hosted setups are acceptable.
- **Role:** the de facto standard benchmark for report generation, so you'll almost certainly need it for comparisons.

**2. CheXpert Plus (Stanford)**
- **Size:** 223K report–image pairs, 188K studies and 65K patients. Reports are split into sections, and the release includes DICOM and PNG images, demographics, CheXpert/CheXbert labels and RadGraph annotations.
- **Access:** register on the Stanford AIMI Shared Datasets site and accept a research-use agreement (non-commercial, no redistribution). It's quicker than PhysioNet because no training course is required.
- **Watch out:** the official test set is tiny (about 200 studies, and only about 61 have a Findings section), so plan your own splits.

**3. ReXGradient-160K (Gradient Health / Rajpurkar lab, 2025)**
- **Size:** 160K studies, about 273K images and about 109K patients from 79 US sites across several health systems. That makes it more diverse than single-hospital sets.
- **Format:** images are PNGs converted from DICOM. GPT-4o was used to split the reports into sections, so the text is sectioned but not raw.
- **Access:** a gated Hugging Face dataset (`rajpurkarlab/ReXGradient-160K`). You accept the license on the dataset page, which is the fastest route here.
- **Splits:** train/validation/public test of 140K/10K/10K, plus a private 10K test set behind the ReXrank leaderboard. A later paper gives slightly larger counts, probably because it includes the private split.

**4. IU X-ray / Open-i (Indiana University, via NLM)**
- **Size:** about 7.5K images and about 3.9K reports with findings and impression.
- **Access:** free download from Open-i with no agreement step.
- **Watch out:** it's small, and de-identification replaced many tokens with "XXXX". It's fine for prototyping and as a second benchmark, but too small to train on alone.

**5. CANDID-PTX (Dunedin, New Zealand)**
- **Size:** about 19K CXRs with free-text reports, focused on pneumothorax, chest tubes and rib fractures.
- **Access:** you need a data use agreement, and typically institutional ethics approval, so it's slower to get.
- **Role:** useful as an out-of-distribution English test set from a non-US site.

## Non-English

**PadChest (Hospital San Juan, Alicante): Spanish**
- **Size:** about 160K images, 67K patients and about 110K reports, with 174 labeled findings mapped to UMLS.
- **Access:** request it through a form on the BIMCV site, agreeing not to share the data or try to re-identify anyone.
- **Watch out:** the release contains report excerpts that were preprocessed, possibly normalized. Check that the text is close enough to the original reports for your generation experiment before you rely on it.
- **PadChest-GR:** a smaller derived set with 4,555 studies and finding-level sentences in both Spanish and English, plus bounding boxes. It's good for grounded or bilingual generation, and you request it through BIMCV too.

**BIMCV-COVID19+ (Valencia)** also includes Spanish reports, but it's narrower (COVID-era cohort).

4. Request PadChest or PadChest-GR for the Spanish experiment.

- **Caption sets:** ROCO and MedPix have figure captions, not clinical reports.

2. Meanwhile, accept the ReXGradient license and register for CheXpert Plus, which are both quick.
3. Train on MIMIC-CXR and/or CheXpert Plus, and test across institutions on ReXGradient and IU X-ray.
4. Request PadChest or PadChest-GR for the Spanish experiment.

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
Five main public datasets pair chest X-rays with the radiologist's actual report text. Four are in English, and PadChest is the main non-English (Spanish) option. Most CXR datasets only release labels extracted from the reports, so the list is short.

## English free-text reports

**1. MIMIC-CXR (Beth Israel Deaconess, Boston)**
- **Size:** about 377K images, 227K studies and 65K patients, with full reports (findings, impression, indication, comparison).
- **Access:** through PhysioNet. You need a credentialed account (ID check plus a reference), the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" human-subjects course, and a signed data use agreement. Expect this to take a few days to a couple of weeks.
- **Files:** the reports are in the MIMIC-CXR DICOM release (`mimic-cxr-reports.zip`). Most people use MIMIC-CXR-JPG for images (about 570 GB) and take the reports from the main release. The full DICOM set is several TB.
- **Watch out:** the PhysioNet agreement forbids sending the data to third-party services. That includes consumer LLM APIs, which matters if you plan to use LLMs for evaluation or report cleanup. PhysioNet has published guidance on which hosted setups are acceptable.
- **Role:** the de facto standard benchmark for report generation, so you'll almost certainly need it for comparisons.

**2. CheXpert Plus (Stanford)**
- **Size:** 223K report–image pairs, 188K studies and 65K patients. Reports are split into sections, and the release includes DICOM and PNG images, demographics, CheXpert/CheXbert labels and RadGraph annotations.
- **Access:** register on the Stanford AIMI Shared Datasets site and accept a research-use agreement (non-commercial, no redistribution). It's quicker than PhysioNet because no training course is required.
- **Watch out:** the official test set is tiny (about 200 studies, and only about 61 have a Findings section), so plan your own splits.

**3. ReXGradient-160K (Gradient Health / Rajpurkar lab, 2025)**
- **Size:** 160K studies, about 273K images and about 109K patients from 79 US sites across several health systems. That makes it more diverse than single-hospital sets.
- **Format:** images are PNGs converted from DICOM. GPT-4o was used to split the reports into sections, so the text is sectioned but not raw.
- **Access:** a gated Hugging Face dataset (`rajpurkarlab/ReXGradient-160K`). You accept the license on the dataset page, which is the fastest route here.
- **Splits:** train/validation/public test of 140K/10K/10K, plus a private 10K test set behind the ReXrank leaderboard. A later paper gives slightly larger counts, probably because it includes the private split.

**4. IU X-ray / Open-i (Indiana University, via NLM)**
- **Size:** about 7.5K images and about 3.9K reports with findings and impression.
- **Access:** free download from Open-i with no agreement step.
- **Watch out:** it's small, and de-identification replaced many tokens with "XXXX". It's fine for prototyping and as a second benchmark, but too small to train on alone.

**5. CANDID-PTX (Dunedin, New Zealand)**
- **Size:** about 19K CXRs with free-text reports, focused on pneumothorax, chest tubes and rib fractures.
- **Access:** you need a data use agreement, and typically institutional ethics approval, so it's slower to get.
- **Role:** useful as an out-of-distribution English test set from a non-US site.

## Non-English

**PadChest (Hospital San Juan, Alicante): Spanish**
- **Size:** about 160K images, 67K patients and about 110K reports, with 174 labeled findings mapped to UMLS.
- **Access:** request it through a form on the BIMCV site, agreeing not to share the data or try to re-identify anyone.
- **Watch out:** the release contains report excerpts that were preprocessed, possibly normalized. Check that the text is close enough to the original reports for your generation experiment before you rely on it.
- **PadChest-GR:** a smaller derived set with 4,555 studies and finding-level sentences in both Spanish and English, plus bounding boxes. It's good for grounded or bilingual generation, and you request it through BIMCV too.

**BIMCV-COVID19+ (Valencia)** also includes Spanish reports, but it's narrower (COVID-era cohort).

## What to skip
These are often mistaken for report datasets but only release labels or derived annotations:
- **Label-only sets:** ChestX-ray14 (NIH), the original CheXpert, VinDr-CXR and BRAX.
- **MIMIC derivatives:** Chest ImaGenome, MS-CXR and CXR-PRO add annotations or cleaned reports to MIMIC. They need the same PhysioNet credentials and don't add any new patients.
- **Caption sets:** ROCO and MedPix have figure captions, not clinical reports.

## Suggested plan
1. Start the PhysioNet credentialing now, because it has the longest lead time.
2. Meanwhile, accept the ReXGradient license and register for CheXpert Plus, which are both quick.
3. Train on MIMIC-CXR and/or CheXpert Plus, and test across institutions on ReXGradient and IU X-ray.
4. Request PadChest or PadChest-GR for the Spanish experiment.

Judge votes✓ ✓ ✓
Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
Five public datasets have both a skin tone label and a diagnosis for every image, with Fitzpatrick V and VI present in real numbers (hundreds, not a handful). They are **Fitzpatrick17k, DDI, PASSION, DermaCon-IN and SCIN**. Each has a weakness, so for an audit you'd want two or three together. Checked on 12 Nov 2026.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** a skin tone label per image or patient (Fitzpatrick or Monk); a diagnosis per image; Fitzpatrick V and VI in real numbers.
- **Nice to have:** obtainable without your institution signing a data agreement; biopsy- or expert-confirmed labels.
- **Assumed:** you only need research use, not commercial use. Almost all of these are non-commercial.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Darker skin (V and VI) | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Fitzpatrick17k** | Labels file is open; images via source links or a request form, a few days | CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 | 16,577 images, 114 conditions | about 1,500 type V and 600 type VI | site today; counts from memory |
| 2 | **DDI** (Stanford) | Free account and research agreement, a few days | Stanford research use agreement (non-commercial, from memory) | 656 biopsy-proven images, 570 patients | **207 images of V–VI** (159 benign, 48 malignant) | today |
| 3 | **PASSION** (sub-Saharan Africa, children) | Request form, a few days | PASSION licence: non-commercial, no reposting | 4,901 images, 1,653 patients | types III–VI only; the test split alone has 341 type V and 88 type VI images | today |
| 4 | **DermaCon-IN** (South India) | Open download on Harvard Dataverse | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | 5,450 images, 3,002 patients, 245 diagnoses | mostly types III–V; number of type VI not confirmed | registry today; the download page blocked my automated check |
| 5 | **SCIN** (Google, US contributors) | Open download | SCIN licence (permissive; bans re-identification) | 10,000+ images, 5,000+ cases | depends on which label you use (see below) | today |

## Details
1. **[Fitzpatrick17k](https://github.com/mattgroh/fitzpatrick17k)** is clinical photos from two online dermatology atlases, Atlas Dermatologico and DermaAmin. Each image has a single Fitzpatrick type (I–VI) and a diagnosis, so it has the most type V–VI images of anything here. The skin types were judged from the photos by crowd annotators, and the diagnosis labels are known to be noisy. The repo has the label file and image links, and some links are broken. For the full image set there is a request form. Reference: Groh et al. 2021.
2. **[DDI](https://aimi.stanford.edu/datasets/ddi-diverse-dermatology-images)** was built for exactly this kind of comparison. Its V–VI images are matched to I–II images by diagnosis, age, sex and photo date. All diagnoses are confirmed by biopsy. Skin type comes only in three groups (I–II, III–IV, V–VI), and it is small. Its authors found that commercial and published models did worse on V–VI ([arXiv 2203.08807](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.08807)), which gives you a ready baseline. To get it, register at Stanford AIMI, accept the agreement and download from the link on that page.
3. **[PASSION](https://passionderm.github.io/)** is phone photos of children in Madagascar, Guinea, Malawi and Tanzania. Labels are Fitzpatrick type, a diagnosis (eczema, fungal infection, scabies or "other", with ICD-10 and ICD-11 codes across 44 conditions), plus body site, age and sex. It has a fixed train/test split by patient. Since there are no type I–II patients, use it as an external darker-skin test set, not for a light-versus-dark comparison within the dataset. The authors' baseline scored a balanced accuracy of 0.70 on type V and 0.73 on type VI ([MICCAI 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04584v1)).
4. **[DermaCon-IN](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/W7OUZM)** is the only clinical dataset here with **both Fitzpatrick and Monk** labels on every image. Four dermatologists labelled the diagnoses; where two of them labelled the same images, they agreed well (kappa 0.84). The paper is inconsistent about which skin types it covers: in one place IV–VI, in another III–IV. Check the distribution after downloading ([paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.06099)).
5. **[SCIN](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/scin)** comes with three tone labels:
   - Self-reported: V is 9.8% and VI is 6.6%.
   - Dermatologist estimate: V is 5.3% and VI is only 0.6%.
   - Monk scale from two lay graders (one in the US, one in India): 8 and above is under 1%.

   Diagnoses are dermatologists' differentials from the photos, with no biopsy. It is useful mostly as a Monk-scale check, or if you're comfortable relying on self-reported type ([paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.18545)).

## Known, not confirmed
- **UNICAMP "Black skin lesions"** ([Zenodo 10570316](https://zenodo.org/records/10570316)) is acral lesions (palms, soles, nails) assessed against the Fitzpatrick scale. It's available on request with an institutional email, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. I couldn't confirm the image count or the skin type spread.

## Not recommended, and why
- **MRA-MIDAS:** only about 2 type VI patients out of 796 ([NEJM AI](https://ai.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/AIdbp2400732)).
- **DDI-2:** patients who self-identified as Asian; a recent preprint reports no type V–VI cancers in it.
- **PAD-UFES-20:** has Fitzpatrick labels, but nearly all are types I–III.
- **HAM10000 and ISIC:** no consistent per-image skin type, and overwhelmingly light skin.
- **SkinCAP:** a captioned subset of Fitzpatrick17k and DDI, so no new images.

## What I could not find
No public skin-cancer dataset has many **biopsy-confirmed cancers on type V–VI skin**; DDI's 48 is the most. Darker-skin coverage elsewhere is mostly inflammatory and infectious conditions. The registry searches turned up mostly noise; the useful finds came from the literature and the web.

## Next step
For the audit, I'd use DDI as the biopsy-confirmed core, Fitzpatrick17k for statistical power across all six types, and PASSION and DermaCon-IN as external tests on darker skin. Add SCIN if you want the Monk scale. You can start on DermaCon-IN, SCIN and the Fitzpatrick17k labels today, and send the DDI and PASSION requests now.

Everything is in an interactive page you can filter and compare: `/private/tmp/e-do23Oy/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`

Sources: [PASSION](https://passionderm.github.io/), [PASSION paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04584v1), [DermaCon-IN paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.06099), [SCIN repo](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/scin), [SCIN paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.18545), [DDI](https://aimi.stanford.edu/datasets/ddi-diverse-dermatology-images), [DDI-2](https://github.com/DaneshjouLab/ddi2-dataset), [Fitzpatrick17k](https://github.com/mattgroh/fitzpatrick17k), [MIDAS](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.06.27.24309562v1.full), [Global Atlas of Digital Dermatology](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.00840)

They are **Fitzpatrick17k, DDI, PASSION, DermaCon-IN and SCIN**. Each has a weakness, so for an audit you'd want two or three together. Checked on 12 Nov 2026.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** a skin tone label per image or patient (Fitzpatrick or Monk); a diagnosis per image; Fitzpatrick V and VI in real numbers.
- **Nice to have:** obtainable without your institution signing a data agreement; biopsy- or expert-confirmed labels.
- **Assumed:** you only need research use, not commercial use. Almost all of these are non-commercial.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Darker skin (V and VI) | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Fitzpatrick17k** | Labels file is open; images via source links or a request form, a few days | CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 | 16,577 images, 114 conditions | about 1,500 type V and 600 type VI | site today; counts from memory |
| 2 | **DDI** (Stanford) | Free account and research agreement, a few days | Stanford research use agreement (non-commercial, from memory) | 656 biopsy-proven images, 570 patients | **207 images of V–VI** (159 benign, 48 malignant) | today |
| 3 | **PASSION** (sub-Saharan Africa, children) | Request form, a few days | PASSION licence: non-commercial, no reposting | 4,901 images, 1,653 patients | types III–VI only; the test split alone has 341 type V and 88 type VI images | today |
| 4 | **DermaCon-IN** (South India) | Open download on Harvard Dataverse | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | 5,450 images, 3,002 patients, 245 diagnoses | mostly types III–V; number of type VI not confirmed | registry today; the download page blocked my automated check |
| 5 | **SCIN** (Google, US contributors) | Open download | SCIN licence (permissive; bans re-identification) | 10,000+ images, 5,000+ cases | depends on which label you use (see below) | today |

## Details
1. **[Fitzpatrick17k](https://github.com/mattgroh/fitzpatrick17k)** is clinical photos from two online dermatology atlases, Atlas Dermatologico and DermaAmin. Each image has a single Fitzpatrick type (I–VI) and a diagnosis, so it has the most type V–VI images of anything here. The skin types were judged from the photos by crowd annotators, and the diagnosis labels are known to be noisy. The repo has the label file and image links, and some links are broken. For the full image set there is a request form. Reference: Groh et al. 2021.
2. **[DDI](https://aimi.stanford.edu/datasets/ddi-diverse-dermatology-images)** was built for exactly this kind of comparison. Its V–VI images are matched to I–II images by diagnosis, age, sex and photo date. All diagnoses are confirmed by biopsy. Skin type comes only in three groups (I–II, III–IV, V–VI), and it is small. Its authors found that commercial and published models did worse on V–VI ([arXiv 2203.08807](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.08807)), which gives you a ready baseline. To get it, register at Stanford AIMI, accept the agreement and download from the link on that page.
3. **[PASSION](https://passionderm.github.io/)** is phone photos of children in Madagascar, Guinea, Malawi and Tanzania. Labels are Fitzpatrick type, a diagnosis (eczema, fungal infection, scabies or "other", with ICD-10 and ICD-11 codes across 44 conditions), plus body site, age and sex. It has a fixed train/test split by patient. Since there are no type I–II patients, use it as an external darker-skin test set, not for a light-versus-dark comparison within the dataset. The authors' baseline scored a balanced accuracy of 0.70 on type V and 0.73 on type VI ([MICCAI 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04584v1)).
4. **[DermaCon-IN](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/W7OUZM)** is the only clinical dataset here with **both Fitzpatrick and Monk** labels on every image. Four dermatologists labelled the diagnoses; where two of them labelled the same images, they agreed well (kappa 0.84). The paper is inconsistent about which skin types it covers: in one place IV–VI, in another III–IV. Check the distribution after downloading ([paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.06099)).
5. **[SCIN](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/scin)** comes with three tone labels:
   - Self-reported: V is 9.8% and VI is 6.6%.
   - Dermatologist estimate: V is 5.3% and VI is only 0.6%.
   - Monk scale from two lay graders (one in the US, one in India): 8 and above is under 1%.

   Diagnoses are dermatologists' differentials from the photos, with no biopsy. It is useful mostly as a Monk-scale check, or if you're comfortable relying on self-reported type ([paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.18545)).

## Known, not confirmed
- **UNICAMP "Black skin lesions"** ([Zenodo 10570316](https://zenodo.org/records/10570316)) is acral lesions (palms, soles, nails) assessed against the Fitzpatrick scale. It's available on request with an institutional email, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. I couldn't confirm the image count or the skin type spread.

## Not recommended, and why
- **MRA-MIDAS:** only about 2 type VI patients out of 796 ([NEJM AI](https://ai.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/AIdbp2400732)).
- **DDI-2:** patients who self-identified as Asian; a recent preprint reports no type V–VI cancers in it.
- **PAD-UFES-20:** has Fitzpatrick labels, but nearly all are types I–III.
- **HAM10000 and ISIC:** no consistent per-image skin type, and overwhelmingly light skin.
- **SkinCAP:** a captioned subset of Fitzpatrick17k and DDI, so no new images.

## What I could not find
No public skin-cancer dataset has many **biopsy-confirmed cancers on type V–VI skin**; DDI's 48 is the most. Darker-skin coverage elsewhere is mostly inflammatory and infectious conditions. The registry searches turned up mostly noise; the useful finds came from the literature and the web.

## Next step
For the audit, I'd use DDI as the biopsy-confirmed core, Fitzpatrick17k for statistical power across all six types, and PASSION and DermaCon-IN as external tests on darker skin. Add SCIN if you want the Monk scale. You can start on DermaCon-IN, SCIN and the Fitzpatrick17k labels today, and send the DDI and PASSION requests now.

Everything is in an interactive page you can filter and compare: `/private/tmp/e-do23Oy/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
Five public datasets have both a skin tone label and a diagnosis for every image, with Fitzpatrick V and VI present in real numbers (hundreds, not a handful). They are **Fitzpatrick17k, DDI, PASSION, DermaCon-IN and SCIN**. Each has a weakness, so for an audit you'd want two or three together. Checked on 12 Nov 2026.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** a skin tone label per image or patient (Fitzpatrick or Monk); a diagnosis per image; Fitzpatrick V and VI in real numbers.
- **Nice to have:** obtainable without your institution signing a data agreement; biopsy- or expert-confirmed labels.
- **Assumed:** you only need research use, not commercial use. Almost all of these are non-commercial.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Darker skin (V and VI) | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Fitzpatrick17k** | Labels file is open; images via source links or a request form, a few days | CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 | 16,577 images, 114 conditions | about 1,500 type V and 600 type VI | site today; counts from memory |
| 2 | **DDI** (Stanford) | Free account and research agreement, a few days | Stanford research use agreement (non-commercial, from memory) | 656 biopsy-proven images, 570 patients | **207 images of V–VI** (159 benign, 48 malignant) | today |
| 3 | **PASSION** (sub-Saharan Africa, children) | Request form, a few days | PASSION licence: non-commercial, no reposting | 4,901 images, 1,653 patients | types III–VI only; the test split alone has 341 type V and 88 type VI images | today |
| 4 | **DermaCon-IN** (South India) | Open download on Harvard Dataverse | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | 5,450 images, 3,002 patients, 245 diagnoses | mostly types III–V; number of type VI not confirmed | registry today; the download page blocked my automated check |
| 5 | **SCIN** (Google, US contributors) | Open download | SCIN licence (permissive; bans re-identification) | 10,000+ images, 5,000+ cases | depends on which label you use (see below) | today |

## Details
1. **[Fitzpatrick17k](https://github.com/mattgroh/fitzpatrick17k)** is clinical photos from two online dermatology atlases, Atlas Dermatologico and DermaAmin. Each image has a single Fitzpatrick type (I–VI) and a diagnosis, so it has the most type V–VI images of anything here. The skin types were judged from the photos by crowd annotators, and the diagnosis labels are known to be noisy. The repo has the label file and image links, and some links are broken. For the full image set there is a request form. Reference: Groh et al. 2021.
2. **[DDI](https://aimi.stanford.edu/datasets/ddi-diverse-dermatology-images)** was built for exactly this kind of comparison. Its V–VI images are matched to I–II images by diagnosis, age, sex and photo date. All diagnoses are confirmed by biopsy. Skin type comes only in three groups (I–II, III–IV, V–VI), and it is small. Its authors found that commercial and published models did worse on V–VI ([arXiv 2203.08807](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.08807)), which gives you a ready baseline. To get it, register at Stanford AIMI, accept the agreement and download from the link on that page.
3. **[PASSION](https://passionderm.github.io/)** is phone photos of children in Madagascar, Guinea, Malawi and Tanzania. Labels are Fitzpatrick type, a diagnosis (eczema, fungal infection, scabies or "other", with ICD-10 and ICD-11 codes across 44 conditions), plus body site, age and sex. It has a fixed train/test split by patient. Since there are no type I–II patients, use it as an external darker-skin test set, not for a light-versus-dark comparison within the dataset. The authors' baseline scored a balanced accuracy of 0.70 on type V and 0.73 on type VI ([MICCAI 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04584v1)).
4. **[DermaCon-IN](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/W7OUZM)** is the only clinical dataset here with **both Fitzpatrick and Monk** labels on every image. Four dermatologists labelled the diagnoses; where two of them labelled the same images, they agreed well (kappa 0.84). The paper is inconsistent about which skin types it covers: in one place IV–VI, in another III–IV. Check the distribution after downloading ([paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.06099)).
5. **[SCIN](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/scin)** comes with three tone labels:
   - Self-reported: V is 9.8% and VI is 6.6%.
   - Dermatologist estimate: V is 5.3% and VI is only 0.6%.
   - Monk scale from two lay graders (one in the US, one in India): 8 and above is under 1%.

   Diagnoses are dermatologists' differentials from the photos, with no biopsy. It is useful mostly as a Monk-scale check, or if you're comfortable relying on self-reported type ([paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.18545)).

## Known, not confirmed
- **UNICAMP "Black skin lesions"** ([Zenodo 10570316](https://zenodo.org/records/10570316)) is acral lesions (palms, soles, nails) assessed against the Fitzpatrick scale. It's available on request with an institutional email, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. I couldn't confirm the image count or the skin type spread.

## Not recommended, and why
- **MRA-MIDAS:** only about 2 type VI patients out of 796 ([NEJM AI](https://ai.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/AIdbp2400732)).
- **DDI-2:** patients who self-identified as Asian; a recent preprint reports no type V–VI cancers in it.
- **PAD-UFES-20:** has Fitzpatrick labels, but nearly all are types I–III.
- **HAM10000 and ISIC:** no consistent per-image skin type, and overwhelmingly light skin.
- **SkinCAP:** a captioned subset of Fitzpatrick17k and DDI, so no new images.

## What I could not find
No public skin-cancer dataset has many **biopsy-confirmed cancers on type V–VI skin**; DDI's 48 is the most. Darker-skin coverage elsewhere is mostly inflammatory and infectious conditions. The registry searches turned up mostly noise; the useful finds came from the literature and the web.

## Next step
For the audit, I'd use DDI as the biopsy-confirmed core, Fitzpatrick17k for statistical power across all six types, and PASSION and DermaCon-IN as external tests on darker skin. Add SCIN if you want the Monk scale. You can start on DermaCon-IN, SCIN and the Fitzpatrick17k labels today, and send the DDI and PASSION requests now.
