## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** raw standard 12-lead resting ECG waveforms, about 10 seconds each
- **R2 (must):** labels for atrial fibrillation (AF), right and left bundle branch block (RBBB, LBBB) and AV block
- **R3 (must):** at least a few thousand recordings
- **R4 (must):** a free download this week, with no application, data use agreement (DUA) or credentialing
- **R5 (nice to have):** labels assigned or confirmed by cardiologists
- I assumed research use with no commercial restriction needed. All the top sets are CC BY 4.0 anyway.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | PTB-XL | open download, minutes | CC BY 4.0 | 21,799 ECGs, 3.2 GB | strong; cardiologist labels | today |
| 2 | Chapman-Shaoxing + Ningbo (large-scale 12-lead arrhythmia DB) | open download, minutes | CC BY 4.0 | 45,152 ECGs, 5.5 GB | strong; labelled by physicians, second physician checked | today |
| 3 | PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2021 | open download, minutes | CC BY 4.0 | ~88k ECGs, 13.6 GB | strong; adds CPSC 2018 and Georgia | today (contents from memory) |
| 4 | SPH (Shandong Provincial Hospital) | open download from figshare | CC BY 4.0 | 25,770 ECGs | strong | licence today; download page from memory |
| 5 | CODE-15% | open download, minutes | CC BY 4.0 | 345,779 exams, 46 GB | partial; noisier labels | today |
| 6 | CODE-test | open download, minutes | CC BY 4.0 | 827 ECGs | test set only; cardiologist consensus | today |
| 7 | MIMIC-IV-ECG | open download | ODbL | ~800k ECGs, 97 GB | partial; machine labels | today |
| 8 | PTB-XL+ | open download | CC BY 4.0 | same records as PTB-XL | add-on | today |

## Details
1. **PTB-XL** — https://physionet.org/content/ptb-xl/1.0.3/
   - **Contents:** 10-second ECGs at 500 Hz and 100 Hz, labelled with SCP-ECG codes. The codes include AFIB, CRBBB, CLBBB, IRBBB, LAFB and first-, second- and third-degree AV block.
   - **Who labelled them:** the page says the waveforms were "annotated by up to two cardiologists" and "a large fraction … validated by a second cardiologist".
   - **Caveat:** some labels started as automatic device interpretations, so filter on the `validated_by_human` flag.
   - **Split:** it comes with patient-wise folds (folds 1–8 to train, 9 to validate, 10 to test). Use them.
   - **Limits:** recorded in Germany in 1989–96.
2. **Chapman-Shaoxing + Ningbo** — https://physionet.org/content/ecg-arrhythmia/1.0.0/
   - **Contents:** 45,152 ten-second ECGs with SNOMED CT labels.
   - **Who labelled them:** "a licensed physician labeled… another licensed physician performed a secondary validation… a senior physician" settled disagreements. The page doesn't say they were cardiologists.
   - It replaces the original 10,646-record figshare release from 2020.
   - From memory, people have reported some label noise, so inspect the rare classes.
3. **Challenge 2021** — https://physionet.org/content/challenge-2021/1.0.3/
   - The useful extra parts are CPSC 2018 (6,877 records labelled for AF, first-degree AV block, LBBB and RBBB, 6–60 s long) and Georgia (10,344 ten-second records). The labels are already mapped to a common code set, and scoring code is included.
   - **Overlap warning:** it also contains PTB-XL and Chapman/Ningbo. Remove the duplicates before combining it with #1 or #2, or records will leak between training and test.
4. **SPH** — DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.c.5779802. The paper is Liu et al. 2022, *Scientific Data*, doi:10.1038/s41597-022-01403-5.
   - **Contents:** 25,770 ECGs, 10–60 seconds long (crop them to 10 s), with standardised AHA diagnostic statements.
   - figshare blocked my automated check, so the open download is from memory. Who wrote the labels is also unconfirmed; check the paper.
5. **CODE-15%** — https://zenodo.org/records/4916206
   - **Contents:** Brazilian telehealth ECGs labelled for first-degree AV block, RBBB, LBBB, sinus bradycardia, AF and sinus tachycardia.
   - From memory, the labels come semi-automatically from cardiologist reports, and there is no label for second- or third-degree block.
   - Best used for pretraining. It was used in Ribeiro et al. 2020, *Nature Communications*, doi:10.1038/s41467-020-15432-4.
6. **CODE-test** — https://zenodo.org/records/3765780
   - Two cardiologists labelled every ECG and "a third senior specialist" settled disagreements.
   - Use it as an independent gold-standard test set.
7. **MIMIC-IV-ECG** — https://physionet.org/content/mimic-iv-ecg/1.0/
   - The open release has only machine-generated report text, which you'd have to parse into labels.
   - The labels derived from clinical records (MIMIC-IV-ECG-Ext-ICD) need credentialing.
8. **PTB-XL+** — https://physionet.org/content/ptb-xl-plus/1.0.1/
   - Adds ECG features and labels from two commercial interpretation algorithms to every PTB-XL record. Useful as a comparison baseline, not as new recordings.

## Known, not confirmed
- **SPH:** the access terms and who labelled it (see #4).
- **Challenge sets:** the exact record counts and which classes are scored are from memory.

## Not recommended, and why
- **KURIAS-ECG** (Korean): a good clinical fit, but the page says "only registered users who sign the specified data use agreement can access the files". It's a personal click-through agreement, not one your institution signs. Use it only if your no-DUA rule allows that.
- **MIT-BIH AF Database and PhysioNet Challenge 2017:** these are 2-lead Holter and single-lead recordings, not 12-lead resting ECGs.
- **PTB Diagnostic** (only 549 records, mostly heart attacks), **Leipzig** (children and congenital heart disease) and **MedalCare-XL** (simulated ECGs).
- **Full CODE and UK Biobank:** need an application (from memory).
- **Hugging Face copies of these datasets:** unofficial copies. Download from the official sources.

## What I could not find
Apart from PTB-XL and CODE-test, I found no large open set where every label was confirmed by a cardiologist. Second- and third-degree AV block are rare in every dataset, so expect a few hundred examples at most once you pool them.

## Next step
1. Today, download PTB-XL and CODE-test.
2. Add Chapman/Ningbo and CPSC/Georgia from Challenge 2021, removing records that appear in more than one set.
3. Map everything to the SNOMED codes the Challenge uses.
4. Even though this data is open and de-identified, ask your institution's ethics board whether it needs a short "not human subjects research" decision before you publish.

The interactive version of this list, where you can filter and export an access plan, is at `/private/tmp/e-F4cWzl/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

judge votes: PASS PASS PASS

Judge votes✓ ✓ ✓
Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
You have several good options that need no credentialing. Your three targets (AF, bundle branch blocks and AV block) are among the best-labeled findings in public ECG data.

## Top picks

**1. PTB-XL (PhysioNet). Start here.**
- About 21,800 10-second 12-lead ECGs from about 18,900 patients, at 500 Hz and 100 Hz.
- Open access under CC BY 4.0. You can download it directly or with `wget` from physionet.org.
- Labels are SCP-ECG statements written by up to two cardiologists. A `validated_by_human` flag tells you which reports were checked by a person.
- It includes AFIB, CLBBB, CRBBB, IRBBB, LAFB/LPFB, IVCD, 1AVB, 2AVB and 3AVB.
- It comes with recommended patient-level folds (`strat_fold`), and folds 9 and 10 have the highest label quality. That makes it the standard benchmark, so your results will be comparable to published work.

**2. CODE-15% (Zenodo, Ribeiro et al.). Very close to your exact target set.**
- About 346,000 exams from about 234,000 Brazilian patients. Recordings are 7–10 seconds at 400 Hz.
- CC BY 4.0, direct download.
- The labels are exactly 1st-degree AV block, RBBB, LBBB, sinus bradycardia, AF and sinus tachycardia.
- The caveat is that training labels came from automated analysis (Glasgow and Minnesota) combined with the cardiologist's text report. They are good but not individually confirmed.
- **Pair it with the CODE test set** (also on Zenodo): 827 ECGs annotated by consensus of 2–3 cardiologists, with the same six labels. It's a clean held-out evaluation set.

**3. Chapman-Shaoxing / Ningbo (PhysioNet: "A large scale 12-lead electrocardiogram database for arrhythmia study")**
- About 45,000 10-second 12-lead ECGs at 500 Hz, open access.
- Labeled by physicians using SNOMED-CT codes, with strong rhythm coverage including AF, atrial flutter and SVT, plus AV blocks and BBBs.
- Early versions had some known label errors, so use the latest version.

## Also worth knowing
- **PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2021 data:** open access, about 88,000 recordings combining PTB-XL, Chapman, Ningbo, Georgia (about 10,000 10-second ECGs) and CPSC 2018. Everything is already mapped to SNOMED-CT, which saves harmonization work. Watch out for two things: PTB-XL and Chapman are included in it, so don't count them twice, and CPSC and INCART recordings aren't 10 seconds long.
- **SPH / Shandong Provincial Hospital (figshare, CC BY 4.0):** about 25,800 ECGs with AHA-standard statements from physicians.
- **MIMIC-IV-ECG:** about 800,000 ECGs, and the waveforms are openly downloadable. However, the open part only has machine-generated reports. The cardiologist reports are in the credentialed part of MIMIC, so it's useful for pretraining but not for your labels.

## Practical cautions
- **Rare classes:** 2nd- and 3rd-degree AV block have only tens of examples per dataset. Plan to combine datasets or treat "high-grade AV block" as one class.
- **Split by patient**, not by recording, to avoid leakage.
- **Harmonize across datasets:** sampling rate (400 vs 500 Hz), units and lead order. Map labels to SNOMED-CT, using the Challenge 2021 mapping tables.
- **Ethics:** "open access" removes the data use agreement, but your institution may still want an IRB "not human subjects research" determination for de-identified public data. It's usually quick, so it's worth a short email now.

**My recommendation:** train and validate on PTB-XL, add Chapman/Ningbo for more AF and conduction cases, and use the CODE test set as a cardiologist-confirmed external test.

I gave these sizes and license terms from memory and didn't check the live pages, so confirm them on each download page before you rely on them.

Several good datasets fit your constraints. All of the ones below can be downloaded directly with no credentialing or data use agreement, and most are 12-lead with labels from cardiologists or physicians. I'm going from memory here rather than live pages, so check the license and terms on each download page before you commit.

## Top picks

**1. PTB-XL (PhysioNet), my first choice**
- 21,799 recordings, 10 s, 12-lead, 500 Hz (100 Hz copy included), from 18,869 patients.
- Labeled with SCP-ECG statements by up to two cardiologists, with a likelihood score per statement. The labels include `AFIB`, `AFLT`, `CLBBB`, `CRBBB`, `ILBBB`, `IRBBB`, `1AVB`, `2AVB` and `3AVB`.
- It comes with recommended stratified folds (use fold 9 for validation and fold 10 for test, which have the highest label quality). That makes your results comparable to published work.
- License: CC BY 4.0. You can get it with `wget -r -N -c -np https://physionet.org/files/ptb-xl/1.0.3/` or download the zip.

**2. Chapman-Shaoxing + Ningbo ("A large scale 12-lead ECG database for arrhythmia study", PhysioNet)**
- About 45,000 recordings, 10 s, 12-lead, 500 Hz. Labels were assigned by physicians and reviewed by cardiologists.
- It has plenty of AF and atrial flutter, plus AV block and bundle branch block labels.
- Some records have known quality problems, such as flat-line leads and a few mislabeled files. Screen the signals before training.

**3. CODE-15% (Zenodo)**
- About 345,000 exams from about 233,000 Brazilian patients. Recordings are roughly 7–10 s, 12-lead, 400 Hz.
- Its 6 labels line up closely with your targets: **1st-degree AV block, RBBB, LBBB, AF**, sinus bradycardia and sinus tachycardia.
- The training labels come from cardiologist text reports combined with automated analysis, so they're somewhat noisier. A separate **CODE test set** of 827 exams is annotated by 2–3 cardiologists, which makes it a good external test set.
- License: CC BY 4.0. The full CODE dataset requires an application, but the 15% subset doesn't.

**4. PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2020/2021 training data**
- About 88,000 recordings from several sources (CPSC 2018, CPSC-Extra, Georgia, PTB-XL, Chapman, Ningbo, and others), all mapped to SNOMED-CT codes. It's useful when you want one harmonized label space.
- **CPSC 2018** (about 6,900 recordings) is an especially good fit: its 9 classes include Normal, AF, I-AVB, LBBB and RBBB. Its recordings run 6–60 s, though, not a fixed 10 s.
- **Georgia** (about 10,000 recordings, 10 s) comes from a different population (US Southeast), so it's useful as an external validation site.
- Watch for overlaps: PTB-XL and Chapman/Ningbo are included inside the Challenge set. Don't count them twice or let them leak across your splits.

## Things to plan for
- **High-grade AV block is rare everywhere.** PTB-XL has only around a dozen or so records each of 2nd- and 3rd-degree AVB, and CODE and CPSC only label 1st-degree. You'll probably need to pool several sources, or merge 2nd- and 3rd-degree into a single "high-grade AVB" class.
- **Harmonize the labels early.** Map everything to SNOMED-CT, as the Challenge did, and decide whether incomplete RBBB/LBBB count as bundle branch block.
- **Validate across sites.** For example, train on PTB-XL + Chapman, then test on Georgia and the CODE test set. Models often look much worse on data from a new site.
- **Split by patient.** PTB-XL and CODE have patient IDs, so keep each patient's recordings in one split.
- **Check with your institution about ethics.** Even with public, de-identified data, many institutions want a quick "not human subjects research" determination. It's usually fast, and it's worth asking now so it doesn't hold up publication later.

**Avoid for now:** MIMIC-IV-ECG. Its waveforms are openly downloadable, but its free-text statements are machine-generated, and the cardiologist reports sit in credentialed MIMIC-IV-Note.

My suggestion: start with PTB-XL this week, since it's clean, well documented and has a standard benchmark. Then add Chapman/Ningbo and CODE-15% for more training data, and keep Georgia and the CODE test set for external testing.

I haven't re-checked the dataset pages today, so confirm each one is still listed as "Open Access" before you plan around it.

## Top recommendations

**1. PTB-XL (PhysioNet), the best match**
- 21,799 recordings from 18,869 patients. All are 10 s, 12-lead, at 500 Hz (a 100 Hz version is included).
- Labels are SCP-ECG statements made by up to two cardiologists, with a flag showing whether a human validated each one. That matches your "assigned or confirmed by cardiologists" requirement.
- Relevant labels: AFIB, AFLT, CLBBB, CRBBB, ILBBB/IRBBB, 1AVB, 2AVB, 3AVB, LAFB/LPFB.
- It comes with 10 recommended patient-level folds (folds 9 and 10 have the highest label quality), so your results stay comparable with published benchmarks.
- License is CC BY 4.0. You can download it with `wget -r -N -c -np https://physionet.org/files/ptb-xl/1.0.3/`, about 3 GB. Check the page for the latest version number.

**2. PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2020/2021 training data, for more volume**
- About 88,000 12-lead ECGs from several sources, all mapped to one shared SNOMED-CT label set covering AF, AFL, LBBB, RBBB, IRBBB, 1st-degree AV block, and more.
- The sources are PTB-XL, Chapman-Shaoxing, Ningbo, CPSC 2018, the Georgia 12-lead database (about 10,000 US recordings) and the older PTB/INCART sets.
- Data from several hospitals lets you test how well a model trained at one site works at another, which reviewers care about.
- Caveats: CPSC recordings run 6–60 s, so you'll need to crop or pad them; INCART is 30-minute Holter-style data, so leave it out. Label quality also varies by source.

**3. Chapman-Shaoxing / Ningbo (PhysioNet: "A large scale 12-lead electrocardiogram database for arrhythmia study")**
- About 45,000 recordings, 10 s, 500 Hz, labeled by licensed physicians with SNOMED codes, including AV blocks and bundle branch blocks. It's heavy on rhythm labels, which suits AF.

## Things to plan for

- **2nd- and 3rd-degree AV block are rare everywhere.** PTB-XL has only about a dozen examples of each. If high-grade AV block matters to you, pool data across sources, consider grouping the AV block classes, and report how much your confidence intervals widen with so few cases.
- **Split by patient, not by recording.** PTB-XL and CODE have repeat recordings from the same patients.
- **"Open access" still has terms.** CC BY means you must credit the dataset and cite its paper. Your best starting point is **PTB-XL**, plus the **PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2021** collection if you want more data. Both are open access, need no application or credentialing, and match your recording format. I haven't re-checked the dataset pages today, so confirm each one is still listed as "Open Access" before you plan around it.

## Top recommendations

**1. PTB-XL (PhysioNet), the best match**
- 21,799 recordings from 18,869 patients. All are 10 s, 12-lead, at 500 Hz (a 100 Hz version is included).
- Labels are SCP-ECG statements made by up to two cardiologists, with a flag showing whether a human validated each one. That matches your "assigned or confirmed by cardiologists" requirement.
- Relevant labels: AFIB, AFLT, CLBBB, CRBBB, ILBBB/IRBBB, 1AVB, 2AVB, 3AVB, LAFB/LPFB.
- It comes with 10 recommended patient-level folds (folds 9 and 10 have the highest label quality), so your results stay comparable with published benchmarks.
- License is CC BY 4.0. You can download it with `wget -r -N -c -np https://physionet.org/files/ptb-xl/1.0.3/`, about 3 GB. Check the page for the latest version number.

**2. PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2020/2021 training data, for more volume**
- About 88,000 12-lead ECGs from several sources, all mapped to one shared SNOMED-CT label set covering AF, AFL, LBBB, RBBB, IRBBB, 1st-degree AV block, and more.
- The sources are PTB-XL, Chapman-Shaoxing, Ningbo, CPSC 2018, the Georgia 12-lead database (about 10,000 US recordings) and the older PTB/INCART sets.
- Data from several hospitals lets you test how well a model trained at one site works at another, which reviewers care about.
- Caveats: CPSC recordings run 6–60 s, so you'll need to crop or pad them; INCART is 30-minute Holter-style data, so leave it out. Label quality also varies by source.

**3. Chapman-Shaoxing / Ningbo (PhysioNet: "A large scale 12-lead electrocardiogram database for arrhythmia study")**
- About 45,000 recordings, 10 s, 500 Hz, labeled by licensed physicians with SNOMED codes, including AV blocks and bundle branch blocks. It's heavy on rhythm labels, which suits AF.
- License is CC BY 4.0. Note that it overlaps with the Challenge collection above.

**4. CODE-15% (Zenodo), for large-scale pretraining**
- About 345,000 exams from 233,000 Brazilian patients, CC BY 4.0, no application needed.
- It has 6 labels, including AF, 1st-degree AV block, RBBB and LBBB.
- The labels come from automated analysis combined with text reports, not careful cardiologist review, so they're noisier. Recording length also varies (7–10 s).
- The separate CODE-test set (827 exams annotated by several cardiologists) makes a good external test set for these labels.

**Possible addition: MIMIC-IV-ECG.** It has about 800,000 10-s 12-lead ECGs and, as far as I know, the waveforms and machine-generated reports are open access. The labels are machine reports, though, and linking them to clinical data requires credentialing. Treat it as optional.

- **Split by patient, not by recording.** PTB-XL and CODE have repeat recordings from the same patients.
- **"Open access" still has terms.** CC BY means you must credit the dataset and cite its paper. More importantly, many institutions still want a short determination that secondary use of public, de-identified data is "not human subjects research." That's usually a quick form, not a full ethics review, but check with your IRB or ethics office before you publish.

**Suggested setup:** start with PTB-XL for development and benchmarking. Add the Challenge 2021 sources for training volume and testing on unseen hospitals, and use CODE-test as an external check for AF, bundle branch blocks and 1st-degree AV block.
Prompt

I'm starting a project on automatically detecting atrial fibrillation and conduction problems (bundle branch blocks, AV block) from standard 10-second, 12-lead resting ECGs. I need at least a few thousand recordings that come with diagnostic labels, preferably assigned or confirmed by cardiologists. Our lab has no data use agreements or ethics approval set up yet, so it has to be something I can download this week without applying or getting credentialed. What are my best options?

I'd use **NHANES** as the core US source, with **ELSA (England)** and **CHARLS (China)** or **LASI (India)** for the international comparison. If you want the comparison to line up closely, add **HRS** as the US arm for ages 50+. All of these are free and you can have them within minutes to a few days.

**Where these facts come from:** I checked on 2026-11-12. Facts marked "today" came from the survey's own page or documentation. The rest is from memory, and you should check it in the codebooks before relying on it.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** a national sample (an older-adult sample is fine), blood pressure measured by an examiner, a self-reported "ever told you have high blood pressure" question, antihypertensive medication (so treated people with normal readings still count as hypertensive), and survey weights.
- **Nice to have:** you can get the data within a few weeks with no fee.

## Shortlist
| # | Survey | Who's in it | Access | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NHANES** (US) | all ages | direct download, minutes | today |
| 2 | **HRS** (US) | 50+ | free account, minutes | today (via HRS documentation) |
| 3 | **ELSA** (England) | 50+ | free UK Data Service account, 1–2 days | today |
| 4 | **CHARLS** (China) | 45+ | registration plus approval, about 3 days | today (via web search) |
| 5 | **LASI** (India) | 45+ | registration through the Gateway to Global Aging Data | today (via web search) |
| 6 | **KNHANES** (South Korea) | all ages | free registration; the site is mostly in Korean | partly |
| 7 | **WHO SAGE** (6 low- and middle-income countries) | 50+ | registration plus a short request | from memory |
| 8 | **WHO STEPS** (many countries) | 18–69 | account plus a request for each country | partly |

## Details and how to get each one

**1. NHANES**: https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/
- **Variables (seen today):** BP is measured at the mobile exam centre, in file BPXO_L (`BPXOSY1`, `BPXODI1`, …). The awareness question is in BPQ_L: `BPQ020` asks "Have you ever been told by a doctor or other health professional that you had hypertension, also called high blood pressure?" The documentation says you must use the design variables and weights.
- **Steps:** pick a cycle, download the DEMO, BPXO (or BPX) and BPQ `.xpt` files, then merge them on `SEQN`.
- **Licence:** US public domain; cite NCHS.
- **Caveat:** the 2021–23 cycle measured BP with an automatic (oscillometric) device. Earlier cycles used the auscultatory (BPX) method, which matters if you look at trends.
- **Papers using it:** [Gu et al. 2008, AJH](https://doi.org/10.1038/ajh.2008.185) and [Gu et al. 2012, Circulation](https://doi.org/10.1161/circulationaha.112.096156).

**2. HRS**: https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/
- **Content:** since 2006, a random half of the sample gets an enhanced interview with physical measures each wave, including BP. The core interview asks about doctor-diagnosed high BP and medication (from memory).
- **Steps:** register for free, accept the Conditions of Use, and download the core files (Section I) or the RAND HRS longitudinal file.
- **Conditions:** you agree not to try to identify participants and not to pass the data to third parties.
- **Caveats:**
  - Trained interviewers measure BP, not nurses. That's still an objective measurement, but say so in your methods.
  - Each person is measured only every 4 years.
- **Why use it:** it is harmonised with ELSA, CHARLS and LASI through the Gateway to Global Aging Data (g2aging.org), which makes it the cleanest basis for a cross-national comparison.

**3. ELSA**: https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data
- **Access (seen today):** the ELSA site says "End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS"; non-UK users "can request a username."
- **Content (from memory):** nurse visits measure BP in waves 2, 4, 6 and 8/9, with diagnosis and medication questions and nurse-visit weights.
- **Steps:** register with the UK Data Service, accept the End User Licence, and download study SN 5050.

**4. CHARLS**: https://charls.pku.edu.cn/en/
- **Content:** interviewers take three BP readings.
- **Steps:** register, sign the data-use agreement, and you get a password by email after about 3 days.
- **Caveat:** measured BP is confirmed for waves 1–3 (2011, 2013, 2015). Check whether 2018 and later waves have it.

**5. LASI**: https://lasi-india.org/data-instructions
- **Content:** wave 1 (2017–18), about 73,000 people.
- **Steps:** access is through the Gateway to Global Aging Data; registration is free with agreement to the data-use conditions.
- **Paper doing exactly your analysis:** [PLOS Med 2021](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1003740).

**6. KNHANES**: https://knhanes.kdca.go.kr
- **Why consider it:** it is the closest equivalent to NHANES outside the US: all ages, examiner-measured BP, free SAS/SPSS files.
- **Not confirmed:** whether foreign users can register without hurdles. The site and codebooks are largely in Korean.

**7 and 8. WHO SAGE and STEPS**
- **SAGE:** the paper on awareness in 6 countries ([IJE 2014](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyt215)) used it, but its data are from 2007–10.
- **STEPS:** many countries, but only ages 18–69, and access depends on the country.

## Known, not confirmed
I couldn't check these today, but as far as I know they have measured BP plus self-report:
- **Health Survey for England:** the HSE site blocked automated access; data are on the UK Data Service.
- **MHAS** (Mexico), **TILDA** (Ireland) and **ELSI-Brazil:** their sites didn't respond.

## Not recommended
- **NHIS and BRFSS:** self-reported hypertension only.
- **SHARE:** no BP measurement.
- **UK Biobank:** volunteers rather than a national sample, and the application is paid.
- **Canadian Health Measures Survey:** fits on content, but you can only use it inside a Statistics Canada Research Data Centre, which takes months.
- **CLSA:** application with a fee, and the sample isn't strictly representative.

## Next step
Which comparator to pick depends on the framing:
- **All adults:** compare NHANES with KNHANES or HSE.
- **Older adults:** compare HRS (plus NHANES restricted to ages 50+) with ELSA and CHARLS or LASI, using the Gateway harmonised files.

[This 2026 BMC Public Health paper](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-26341-4) looks at gaps in hypertension care across five national ageing cohorts. I haven't checked which cohorts it uses, but it would be worth reading as a template for the older-adult version.

Sources: [CHARLS user guide](https://charls.charlsdata.com/Public/ashelf/public/uploads/document/2011-charls-wave1/application/CHARLS_nationalbaseline_users_guide.pdf), [Gateway: CHARLS](https://g2aging.org/additional-resources/gateway-blog/05a8df66-b9ab-47de-879e-b0bde672798d), [Gateway: LASI](https://g2aging.org/additional-resources/gateway-blog/a1336913-5fb6-4198-b592-3802ef4729e8), [Gateway harmonised data](https://g2aging.org/harmonized-data/get-data), [HRS 2018 data description](https://hrsdata.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/documentation/data-descriptions/1652380440/h18dd.pdf), [HRS public data overview](https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/biblio/OverviewofHRSPublicData.pdf), [KNHANES profile (IJE)](https://academic.oup.com/ije/article/43/1/69/733063), [JKMS 2025](https://jkms.org/pdf/10.3346/jkms.2025.40.e189)

There's an interactive page where you can compare and filter the surveys and export an access plan: `/private/tmp/e-efRboB/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`

- **Must have:** a national sample (an older-adult sample is fine), blood pressure measured by an examiner, a self-reported "ever told you have high blood pressure" question, antihypertensive medication (so treated people with normal readings still count as hypertensive), and survey weights.
- **Nice to have:** you can get the data within a few weeks with no fee.

## Shortlist
| # | Survey | Who's in it | Access | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NHANES** (US) | all ages | direct download, minutes | today |
| 2 | **HRS** (US) | 50+ | free account, minutes | today (via HRS documentation) |
| 3 | **ELSA** (England) | 50+ | free UK Data Service account, 1–2 days | today |
| 4 | **CHARLS** (China) | 45+ | registration plus approval, about 3 days | today (via web search) |
| 5 | **LASI** (India) | 45+ | registration through the Gateway to Global Aging Data | today (via web search) |
| 6 | **KNHANES** (South Korea) | all ages | free registration; the site is mostly in Korean | partly |
| 7 | **WHO SAGE** (6 low- and middle-income countries) | 50+ | registration plus a short request | from memory |
| 8 | **WHO STEPS** (many countries) | 18–69 | account plus a request for each country | partly |

## Details and how to get each one

**1. NHANES**: https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/
- **Variables (seen today):** BP is measured at the mobile exam centre, in file BPXO_L (`BPXOSY1`, `BPXODI1`, …). The awareness question is in BPQ_L: `BPQ020` asks "Have you ever been told by a doctor or other health professional that you had hypertension, also called high blood pressure?" The documentation says you must use the design variables and weights.
- **Steps:** pick a cycle, download the DEMO, BPXO (or BPX) and BPQ `.xpt` files, then merge them on `SEQN`.
- **Licence:** US public domain; cite NCHS.
- **Caveat:** the 2021–23 cycle measured BP with an automatic (oscillometric) device. Earlier cycles used the auscultatory (BPX) method, which matters if you look at trends.
- **Papers using it:** [Gu et al. 2008, AJH](https://doi.org/10.1038/ajh.2008.185) and [Gu et al. 2012, Circulation](https://doi.org/10.1161/circulationaha.112.096156).

**2. HRS**: https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/
- **Content:** since 2006, a random half of the sample gets an enhanced interview with physical measures each wave, including BP. The core interview asks about doctor-diagnosed high BP and medication (from memory).
- **Steps:** register for free, accept the Conditions of Use, and download the core files (Section I) or the RAND HRS longitudinal file.
- **Conditions:** you agree not to try to identify participants and not to pass the data to third parties.
- **Caveats:**
  - Trained interviewers measure BP, not nurses. That's still an objective measurement, but say so in your methods.
  - Each person is measured only every 4 years.
- **Why use it:** it is harmonised with ELSA, CHARLS and LASI through the Gateway to Global Aging Data (g2aging.org), which makes it the cleanest basis for a cross-national comparison.

**3. ELSA**: https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data
- **Access (seen today):** the ELSA site says "End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS"; non-UK users "can request a username."
- **Content (from memory):** nurse visits measure BP in waves 2, 4, 6 and 8/9, with diagnosis and medication questions and nurse-visit weights.
- **Steps:** register with the UK Data Service, accept the End User Licence, and download study SN 5050.

**4. CHARLS**: https://charls.pku.edu.cn/en/
- **Content:** interviewers take three BP readings.
- **Steps:** register, sign the data-use agreement, and you get a password by email after about 3 days.
- **Caveat:** measured BP is confirmed for waves 1–3 (2011, 2013, 2015). Check whether 2018 and later waves have it.

**5. LASI**: https://lasi-india.org/data-instructions
- **Content:** wave 1 (2017–18), about 73,000 people.
- **Steps:** access is through the Gateway to Global Aging Data; registration is free with agreement to the data-use conditions.
- **Paper doing exactly your analysis:** [PLOS Med 2021](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1003740).

**6. KNHANES**: https://knhanes.kdca.go.kr
- **Why consider it:** it is the closest equivalent to NHANES outside the US: all ages, examiner-measured BP, free SAS/SPSS files.
- **Not confirmed:** whether foreign users can register without hurdles. The site and codebooks are largely in Korean.

**7 and 8. WHO SAGE and STEPS**
- **SAGE:** the paper on awareness in 6 countries ([IJE 2014](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyt215)) used it, but its data are from 2007–10.
- **STEPS:** many countries, but only ages 18–69, and access depends on the country.

## Known, not confirmed
I couldn't check these today, but as far as I know they have measured BP plus self-report:
- **Health Survey for England:** the HSE site blocked automated access; data are on the UK Data Service.
- **MHAS** (Mexico), **TILDA** (Ireland) and **ELSI-Brazil:** their sites didn't respond.

## Not recommended
- **NHIS and BRFSS:** self-reported hypertension only.
- **SHARE:** no BP measurement.
- **UK Biobank:** volunteers rather than a national sample, and the application is paid.
- **Canadian Health Measures Survey:** fits on content, but you can only use it inside a Statistics Canada Research Data Centre, which takes months.
- **CLSA:** application with a fee, and the sample isn't strictly representative.

## Next step
Which comparator to pick depends on the framing:
- **All adults:** compare NHANES with KNHANES or HSE.
- **Older adults:** compare HRS (plus NHANES restricted to ages 50+) with ELSA and CHARLS or LASI, using the Gateway harmonised files.

[This 2026 BMC Public Health paper](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-26341-4) looks at gaps in hypertension care across five national ageing cohorts. I haven't checked which cohorts it uses, but it would be worth reading as a template for the older-adult version.

Sources: [CHARLS user guide](https://charls.charlsdata.com/Public/ashelf/public/uploads/document/2011-charls-wave1/application/CHARLS_nationalbaseline_users_guide.pdf), [Gateway: CHARLS](https://g2aging.org/additional-resources/gateway-blog/05a8df66-b9ab-47de-879e-b0bde672798d), [Gateway: LASI](https://g2aging.org/additional-resources/gateway-blog/a1336913-5fb6-4198-b592-3802ef4729e8), [Gateway harmonised data](https://g2aging.org/harmonized-data/get-data), [HRS 2018 data description](https://hrsdata.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/documentation/data-descriptions/1652380440/h18dd.pdf), [HRS public data overview](https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/biblio/OverviewofHRSPublicData.pdf), [KNHANES profile (IJE)](https://academic.oup.com/ije/article/43/1/69/733063), [JKMS 2025](https://jkms.org/pdf/10.3346/jkms.2025.40.e189)

There's an interactive page where you can compare and filter the surveys and export an access plan: `/private/tmp/e-efRboB/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
I'd use **NHANES** as the US source. For the other countries, **ELSA (England)** and either **CHARLS (China)** or **LASI (India)** are the strongest options. All four put measured blood pressure and a "doctor ever told you" question on the same people. HRS, ELSA, CHARLS and LASI are also sister studies, and ready-made cross-country versions of their variables are on the Gateway to Global Aging Data (g2aging.org). That makes the international comparison much easier.

I checked these on 12 Nov 2026. "Today" in the Checked column means I confirmed it from the official page or the study's own documents. "From memory" means I didn't. Access rules change, so re-check before you submit an ethics application.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** a nationally representative sample. Adults of all ages, or 45+/50+, is fine.
- **R2 (must):** blood pressure measured by a nurse, examiner or trained field staff.
- **R3 (must):** a "has a doctor ever told you that you have high blood pressure" question, asked of the same people.
- **R4 (nice to have):** you can get the data within weeks on a student's standing.

## Shortlist
| # | Survey | Access | Who measured BP | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NHANES** (US, all ages) | Direct download, no account | Health technicians at mobile exam centres | today |
| 2 | **HRS** (US, 50+) | Free registration | Trained interviewers, not nurses | today, from HRS documents |
| 3 | **ELSA** (England, 50+) | Free UK Data Service account and End User Licence, ~days | Nurses (waves 2, 4, 6, 8, 9) | today |
| 4 | **CHARLS** (China, 45+) | Registration plus online agreement, approved in ~3 working days | Trained staff, 3 Omron readings | today, from the CHARLS FAQ |
| 5 | **LASI** (India, 45+, ~72,000 people) | Request form plus short proposal (~weeks), or through g2aging.org | Trained staff | today |
| 6 | **KNHANES** (Korea, all ages) | Registration and data request | Examiners | partly |
| 7 | **TILDA** (Ireland, 50+) | Public file through ISSDA (Irish Social Science Data Archive); fuller data by application, possibly with fees | Nurses | today |
| 8 | **Canadian Health Measures Survey** (CHMS) | Only inside Statistics Canada Research Data Centres, ~months | Mobile clinic staff | access rules from memory |

## Details
**1. NHANES** ([wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/))
- **Variables:** BP readings are in the BPX/BPXO files (automated cuff from 2017 onward). The awareness question is BPQ020. I confirmed its wording today: "ever been told by a doctor or other health professional that you had hypertension, also called high blood pressure?" Related items are BPQ030 (told on 2+ visits) and BPQ150 (taking prescribed BP medication).
- **Steps:**
  - Download the DEMO, BPXO and BPQ files for a cycle and merge them on SEQN.
  - Use the exam weights plus the design variables SDMVSTRA and SDMVPSU.
- **Watch out for:**
  - The 2021–2023 cycle used a new sample design, so read the analysis guidelines before pooling it with earlier cycles.
  - The switch from manual to automated BP measurement affects trend analyses.
- **Example paper:** Egan et al., JAMA 2010 ([doi](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2010.650)), uses the standard awareness definition.

**2. HRS** ([New User Guide](https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/new-user-guide/HRS-New-User-Guide-July-2025.pdf), [physical-measures documentation DR-011](https://hrsonline.isr.umich.edu/sitedocs/userg/dr-011.pdf))
- **Variables:** BP was measured with an Omron HEM-780 during the in-person interview from 2006 onward. Each half of the sample is measured every 4 years.
- **Access:** BP is in the public core files and needs only registration. The blood biomarkers need an extra sensitive-data agreement.
- **Weights:** use the physical-measures weights (KPMWGTR for 2006, NPMWGTR for 2012).
- **Watch out for:** interviewers took the readings, not nurses. If your examiners must be nurses, say this in your methods.

**3. ELSA** ([how to access the data](https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data), [nurse visit user guide](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/population-health-sciences/sites/population_health_sciences/files/5050_elsa_waves_2-4-6-8-9_nurse_data_user_guide.pdf))
- **Access:** the ELSA site says: "End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS."
- **Steps:**
  - Register with the UK Data Service. Use your institution's login (UKAMF) if your institution is a member, otherwise request a username.
  - Download study SN 5050, which includes the nurse files, and use the nurse weights.

**4. CHARLS** ([FAQ](https://charls.pku.edu.cn/en/Faq/Frequently_Asked_Questions.htm))
- **Variables:** the question is "Have you ever been diagnosed with hypertension by a doctor?" BP is measured as three Omron HEM-7200 readings.
- **Steps:**
  - Register at charls.pku.edu.cn and sign the online data-use agreement.
  - Activate your account by email, then apply for each dataset. The FAQ says approval takes about 3 working days.
  - Use the official site only, not the unofficial copies that circulate online.
- **Example papers:** [BMJ Open 2016](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2015-009836) compares self-reported and measured hypertension. [BMC Public Health](https://bmcpublichealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12889-019-6753-x) looks at awareness from 2011 to 2015.

**5. LASI** ([request form](https://iipsindia.ac.in/sites/default/files/LASI_DataRequestForm_0.pdf), [cohort profile](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyab266))
- **Variables:** the question is "Has any health professional ever told you that you have hypertension or high blood pressure?"
- **Steps:** email the form, a 500-word description of your topic and a study proposal to datacenter@iipsindia.ac.in. Alternatively, register on g2aging.org for the harmonised version.
- **Example paper:** [PMC8425529](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8425529) covers awareness, treatment and control in India.

**6–8.**
- **KNHANES:** the closest copy of NHANES's design. Literature found in a web search today says the raw data need registration and a request. KNHANES's English page returned a 404 today, and the site is mostly in Korean. I couldn't tell whether researchers outside Korea can register.
- **TILDA:** the site says the data are "only available for access by non-commercial entities." The fuller health data go through the VISTA remote secure environment or on-site desks, and fees may apply. I haven't checked which BP variables are in the public ISSDA file.
- **CHMS:** realistic only if you have a Canadian affiliation.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Health Survey for England:** nurse-measured BP, distributed through the UK Data Service. Its site blocked my automated check. ELSA already includes an HSE baseline ("wave 0").
- **Indonesia Family Life Survey (IFLS):** measured BP, free registration through RAND, from memory. RAND's site blocked the check.
- **WHO SAGE** (six low- and middle-income countries, measured BP): the catalogue page resolves, but I didn't read its access terms.
- **MHAS (Mexico):** measured BP in a subsample only (from memory). I didn't confirm it.

## Not recommended, and why
- **NHIS and BRFSS:** self-reported hypertension only.
- **SHARE:** no measured BP in its core waves (from memory).
- **UK Biobank:** a volunteer cohort, not nationally representative, and fee-based.

## What I could not find
The general dataset registries returned nothing relevant. Every candidate came from my own knowledge, the literature and web searches, which is normal for national surveys.

## Next step
Start downloading NHANES today. At the same time, register with the UK Data Service for ELSA and with CHARLS, which should take a few days. If you'd like India instead of, or as well as, China, send the LASI request now, because it takes the longest. Before you analyse anything, fix one definition of "unaware" across all surveys: measured BP ≥140/90 (or ≥130/80), or on BP medication, but not reporting a diagnosis. Also note how many readings each survey averages, because that differs between them.

The interactive comparison page is at `/private/tmp/e-jq5eMJ/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

I checked these on 12 Nov 2026. "Today" in the Checked column means I confirmed it from the official page or the study's own documents. "From memory" means I didn't. Access rules change, so re-check before you submit an ethics application.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** a nationally representative sample. Adults of all ages, or 45+/50+, is fine.
- **R2 (must):** blood pressure measured by a nurse, examiner or trained field staff.
- **R3 (must):** a "has a doctor ever told you that you have high blood pressure" question, asked of the same people.
- **R4 (nice to have):** you can get the data within weeks on a student's standing.

## Shortlist
| # | Survey | Access | Who measured BP | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NHANES** (US, all ages) | Direct download, no account | Health technicians at mobile exam centres | today |
| 2 | **HRS** (US, 50+) | Free registration | Trained interviewers, not nurses | today, from HRS documents |
| 3 | **ELSA** (England, 50+) | Free UK Data Service account and End User Licence, ~days | Nurses (waves 2, 4, 6, 8, 9) | today |
| 4 | **CHARLS** (China, 45+) | Registration plus online agreement, approved in ~3 working days | Trained staff, 3 Omron readings | today, from the CHARLS FAQ |
| 5 | **LASI** (India, 45+, ~72,000 people) | Request form plus short proposal (~weeks), or through g2aging.org | Trained staff | today |
| 6 | **KNHANES** (Korea, all ages) | Registration and data request | Examiners | partly |
| 7 | **TILDA** (Ireland, 50+) | Public file through ISSDA (Irish Social Science Data Archive); fuller data by application, possibly with fees | Nurses | today |
| 8 | **Canadian Health Measures Survey** (CHMS) | Only inside Statistics Canada Research Data Centres, ~months | Mobile clinic staff | access rules from memory |

## Details
**1. NHANES** ([wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/))
- **Variables:** BP readings are in the BPX/BPXO files (automated cuff from 2017 onward). The awareness question is BPQ020. I confirmed its wording today: "ever been told by a doctor or other health professional that you had hypertension, also called high blood pressure?" Related items are BPQ030 (told on 2+ visits) and BPQ150 (taking prescribed BP medication).
- **Steps:**
  - Download the DEMO, BPXO and BPQ files for a cycle and merge them on SEQN.
  - Use the exam weights plus the design variables SDMVSTRA and SDMVPSU.
- **Watch out for:**
  - The 2021–2023 cycle used a new sample design, so read the analysis guidelines before pooling it with earlier cycles.
  - The switch from manual to automated BP measurement affects trend analyses.
- **Example paper:** Egan et al., JAMA 2010 ([doi](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2010.650)), uses the standard awareness definition.

**2. HRS** ([New User Guide](https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/new-user-guide/HRS-New-User-Guide-July-2025.pdf), [physical-measures documentation DR-011](https://hrsonline.isr.umich.edu/sitedocs/userg/dr-011.pdf))
- **Variables:** BP was measured with an Omron HEM-780 during the in-person interview from 2006 onward. Each half of the sample is measured every 4 years.
- **Access:** BP is in the public core files and needs only registration. The blood biomarkers need an extra sensitive-data agreement.
- **Weights:** use the physical-measures weights (KPMWGTR for 2006, NPMWGTR for 2012).
- **Watch out for:** interviewers took the readings, not nurses. If your examiners must be nurses, say this in your methods.

**3. ELSA** ([how to access the data](https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data), [nurse visit user guide](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/population-health-sciences/sites/population_health_sciences/files/5050_elsa_waves_2-4-6-8-9_nurse_data_user_guide.pdf))
- **Access:** the ELSA site says: "End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS."
- **Steps:**
  - Register with the UK Data Service. Use your institution's login (UKAMF) if your institution is a member, otherwise request a username.
  - Download study SN 5050, which includes the nurse files, and use the nurse weights.

**4. CHARLS** ([FAQ](https://charls.pku.edu.cn/en/Faq/Frequently_Asked_Questions.htm))
- **Variables:** the question is "Have you ever been diagnosed with hypertension by a doctor?" BP is measured as three Omron HEM-7200 readings.
- **Steps:**
  - Register at charls.pku.edu.cn and sign the online data-use agreement.
  - Activate your account by email, then apply for each dataset. The FAQ says approval takes about 3 working days.
  - Use the official site only, not the unofficial copies that circulate online.
- **Example papers:** [BMJ Open 2016](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2015-009836) compares self-reported and measured hypertension. [BMC Public Health](https://bmcpublichealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12889-019-6753-x) looks at awareness from 2011 to 2015.

**5. LASI** ([request form](https://iipsindia.ac.in/sites/default/files/LASI_DataRequestForm_0.pdf), [cohort profile](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyab266))
- **Variables:** the question is "Has any health professional ever told you that you have hypertension or high blood pressure?"
- **Steps:** email the form, a 500-word description of your topic and a study proposal to datacenter@iipsindia.ac.in. Alternatively, register on g2aging.org for the harmonised version.
- **Example paper:** [PMC8425529](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8425529) covers awareness, treatment and control in India.

**6–8.**
- **KNHANES:** the closest copy of NHANES's design. Literature found in a web search today says the raw data need registration and a request. KNHANES's English page returned a 404 today, and the site is mostly in Korean. I couldn't tell whether researchers outside Korea can register.
- **TILDA:** the site says the data are "only available for access by non-commercial entities." The fuller health data go through the VISTA remote secure environment or on-site desks, and fees may apply. I haven't checked which BP variables are in the public ISSDA file.
- **CHMS:** realistic only if you have a Canadian affiliation.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Health Survey for England:** nurse-measured BP, distributed through the UK Data Service. Its site blocked my automated check. ELSA already includes an HSE baseline ("wave 0").
- **Indonesia Family Life Survey (IFLS):** measured BP, free registration through RAND, from memory. RAND's site blocked the check.
- **WHO SAGE** (six low- and middle-income countries, measured BP): the catalogue page resolves, but I didn't read its access terms.
- **MHAS (Mexico):** measured BP in a subsample only (from memory). I didn't confirm it.

## Not recommended, and why
- **NHIS and BRFSS:** self-reported hypertension only.
- **SHARE:** no measured BP in its core waves (from memory).
- **UK Biobank:** a volunteer cohort, not nationally representative, and fee-based.

## What I could not find
The general dataset registries returned nothing relevant. Every candidate came from my own knowledge, the literature and web searches, which is normal for national surveys.

## Next step
Start downloading NHANES today. At the same time, register with the UK Data Service for ELSA and with CHARLS, which should take a few days. If you'd like India instead of, or as well as, China, send the LASI request now, because it takes the longest. Before you analyse anything, fix one definition of "unaware" across all surveys: measured BP ≥140/90 (or ≥130/80), or on BP medication, but not reporting a diagnosis. Also note how many readings each survey averages, because that differs between them.

The interactive comparison page is at `/private/tmp/e-jq5eMJ/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

- **Watch out for:** interviewers took the readings, not nurses. If your examiners must be nurses, say this in your methods.

**3. ELSA** ([how to access the data](https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data), [nurse visit user guide](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/population-health-sciences/sites/population_health_sciences/files/5050_elsa_waves_2-4-6-8-9_nurse_data_user_guide.pdf))
- **Access:** the ELSA site says: "End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS."
- **Steps:**
  - Register with the UK Data Service. Use your institution's login (UKAMF) if your institution is a member, otherwise request a username.
  - Download study SN 5050, which includes the nurse files, and use the nurse weights.

**4. CHARLS** ([FAQ](https://charls.pku.edu.cn/en/Faq/Frequently_Asked_Questions.htm))
- **Variables:** the question is "Have you ever been diagnosed with hypertension by a doctor?" BP is measured as three Omron HEM-7200 readings.
- **Steps:**
  - Register at charls.pku.edu.cn and sign the online data-use agreement.
  - Activate your account by email, then apply for each dataset. The FAQ says approval takes about 3 working days.
  - Use the official site only, not the unofficial copies that circulate online.
- **Example papers:** [BMJ Open 2016](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2015-009836) compares self-reported and measured hypertension. [BMC Public Health](https://bmcpublichealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12889-019-6753-x) looks at awareness from 2011 to 2015.

**5. LASI** ([request form](https://iipsindia.ac.in/sites/default/files/LASI_DataRequestForm_0.pdf), [cohort profile](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyab266))
- **Variables:** the question is "Has any health professional ever told you that you have hypertension or high blood pressure?"
- **Steps:** email the form, a 500-word description of your topic and a study proposal to datacenter@iipsindia.ac.in. Alternatively, register on g2aging.org for the harmonised version.
- **Example paper:** [PMC8425529](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8425529) covers awareness, treatment and control in India.

**6–8.**
- **KNHANES:** the closest copy of NHANES's design. Literature found in a web search today says the raw data need registration and a request. KNHANES's English page returned a 404 today, and the site is mostly in Korean. I couldn't tell whether researchers outside Korea can register.
- **TILDA:** the site says the data are "only available for access by non-commercial entities." The fuller health data go through the VISTA remote secure environment or on-site desks, and fees may apply. I haven't checked which BP variables are in the public ISSDA file.
- **CHMS:** realistic only if you have a Canadian affiliation.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Health Survey for England:** nurse-measured BP, distributed through the UK Data Service. Its site blocked my automated check. ELSA already includes an HSE baseline ("wave 0").
- **Indonesia Family Life Survey (IFLS):** measured BP, free registration through RAND, from memory. RAND's site blocked the check.
- **WHO SAGE** (six low- and middle-income countries, measured BP): the catalogue page resolves, but I didn't read its access terms.
- **MHAS (Mexico):** measured BP in a subsample only (from memory). I didn't confirm it.

## Not recommended, and why
- **NHIS and BRFSS:** self-reported hypertension only.
- **SHARE:** no measured BP in its core waves (from memory).
- **UK Biobank:** a volunteer cohort, not nationally representative, and fee-based.

## What I could not find
The general dataset registries returned nothing relevant. Every candidate came from my own knowledge, the literature and web searches, which is normal for national surveys.

## Next step
Start downloading NHANES today. At the same time, register with the UK Data Service for ELSA and with CHARLS, which should take a few days. If you'd like India instead of, or as well as, China, send the LASI request now, because it takes the longest. Before you analyse anything, fix one definition of "unaware" across all surveys: measured BP ≥140/90 (or ≥130/80), or on BP medication, but not reporting a diagnosis. Also note how many readings each survey averages, because that differs between them.

The interactive comparison page is at `/private/tmp/e-jq5eMJ/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

## Shortlist

| # | Survey | Who measures BP | How you get it | Time | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NHANES** (US, all ages) | Certified examiners in a mobile exam centre | Free download, no login | minutes | today |
| 2 | **HRS** (US, 50+) | Trained interviewers in the home, not nurses | Free registration | minutes | HRS documentation, via search |
| 3 | **ELSA** (England, 50+) | Nurse visit | Free UK Data Service account | minutes–days | today |
| 4 | **CHARLS** (China, 45+) | Trained staff, 3 readings | Free registration and request | days | CHARLS documentation, via search |
| 5 | **LASI** (India, 45+) | Trained field staff | Request form with ID, reviewed in 24–48 h | days | today |
| 6 | **KNHANES** (Korea, all ages) | Examiners, NHANES-style | Free registration | days | papers' data statements |
| 7 | TILDA (Ireland, 50+) | Nurse health assessment | Application, non-commercial users only | weeks | today |
| 8 | CHMS (Canada) | Mobile clinic | Research Data Centre only | months | today |

## How to get each one

**1. NHANES.** Go to https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/ and download the public files for each cycle you want. For Aug 2021–Aug 2023 these are `DEMO_L`, `BPXO_L` and `BPQ_L`; merge them on `SEQN`.
- **BP:** three Omron readings taken by certified examiners after 5 minutes of seated rest, in the file `BPXO_L` (confirmed today).
- **Awareness:** `BPQ020`, "ever told by a doctor or other health professional that you had hypertension". `BPQ150` asks about current medication.
- **Weights:** use the exam (MEC) weights and the design variables (`SDMVPSU`, `SDMVSTRA`).
- **Caveat:** NHANES stopped mercury (auscultatory) measurements after 2017–18. If you pool cycles across that change, you need to handle the device switch.
- **Use:** the "Awareness of having hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia among US adults: NHANES 2011–2018" paper measures exactly your outcome.

**2. HRS.** Register for free at hrsdata.isr.umich.edu. Public data "only require you to register, log in, and access." Download the core health section (C) and physical measures section (I) for each wave, plus the tracker file for the weights. A cleaned, harmonised version is also on g2aging.org.
- **Who is measured:** since 2006 a random half of respondents gets the enhanced face-to-face interview each wave. That means each person is measured every 4 years.
- **Weights:** use the physical-measures weights.
- **2020 wave:** COVID disrupted the 2020 measurements, so skip it.
- **Caveat:** interviewers take the readings, not nurses. Say so in your methods.

**3. ELSA.** The ELSA site says "End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS" (confirmed today). Log in through your institution (UK Access Management Federation) or request a username if you're outside the UK. Then download the ELSA series, including the nurse files.
- **Nurse visits:** only every other wave (2, 4, 6, 8/9, from memory). COVID affected later waves.
- **Wave 0:** this is the Health Survey for England, which also has nurse-measured BP for all ages.

**4. CHARLS.** The documentation says the data are "freely available to all bona fide researchers." You register at charls.pku.edu.cn/en and submit a request. The site timed out from here, so check the current form yourself.
- **Waves:** use 2011–2018. The 2020 wave apparently had no physical exam, but I couldn't confirm that.
- **Use:** there is a CHARLS paper on hypertension awareness ([PMC6480849](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6480849/)).

**5. LASI.** Fill in the request form at https://www.iipsindia.ac.in/content/lasi-data and attach "a valid identity proof." Access is "only granted for legitimate academic research purposes", and IIPS reviews requests "within 24 to 48 hours" (all confirmed today). With about 73,000 respondents it gives a high-undiagnosed contrast to the US and England.

**6. KNHANES.** Register on knhanes.kdca.go.kr, accept the data use policy and download the raw files. The registration pages are mostly in Korean, and I couldn't confirm that foreign researchers can sign up.

## Not recommended
- **NHIS and BRFSS:** self-reported hypertension only, so they fail your main requirement.
- **SHARE:** as far as I recall, no BP measurement in the main survey.
- **MHAS (Mexico):** BP was measured only in a subsample, from memory, and I couldn't confirm the site.
- **TILDA and CHMS:** they fit the measurement requirement, but access is slower. TILDA needs an application and is for non-commercial users only. CHMS can only be used inside a Canadian Research Data Centre.

## Two things for your methods
- **Who did the measuring differs:** examiners (NHANES), nurses (ELSA) and trained interviewers or field staff (HRS, CHARLS, LASI). Say this in your methods.
- **A single visit overestimates hypertension:** every survey here measures BP on one occasion, not over repeated visits. The usual approach is to define hypertension as a measured BP of 140/90 or higher, or currently taking BP medication. Then estimate unawareness as the share of those people who were never told they have it.

## Next step
Start with NHANES 2017–2020 or 2021–2023 today. Register for ELSA and either CHARLS or LASI this week, since both are free or quick. The Harmonized HRS, ELSA, CHARLS and LASI files on g2aging.org save a lot of variable matching.

**4. CHARLS.** The documentation says the data are "freely available to all bona fide researchers." You register at charls.pku.edu.cn/en and submit a request. The site timed out from here, so check the current form yourself.
- **Waves:** use 2011–2018. The 2020 wave apparently had no physical exam, but I couldn't confirm that.
- **Use:** there is a CHARLS paper on hypertension awareness ([PMC6480849](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6480849/)).

**5. LASI.** Fill in the request form at https://www.iipsindia.ac.in/content/lasi-data and attach "a valid identity proof." Access is "only granted for legitimate academic research purposes", and IIPS reviews requests "within 24 to 48 hours" (all confirmed today). With about 73,000 respondents it gives a high-undiagnosed contrast to the US and England.

**6. KNHANES.** Register on knhanes.kdca.go.kr, accept the data use policy and download the raw files. The registration pages are mostly in Korean, and I couldn't confirm that foreign researchers can sign up.

## Not recommended
- **NHIS and BRFSS:** self-reported hypertension only, so they fail your main requirement.
- **SHARE:** as far as I recall, no BP measurement in the main survey.
- **MHAS (Mexico):** BP was measured only in a subsample, from memory, and I couldn't confirm the site.
- **TILDA and CHMS:** they fit the measurement requirement, but access is slower. TILDA needs an application and is for non-commercial users only. CHMS can only be used inside a Canadian Research Data Centre.

## Two things for your methods
- **Who did the measuring differs:** examiners (NHANES), nurses (ELSA) and trained interviewers or field staff (HRS, CHARLS, LASI). Say this in your methods.
- **A single visit overestimates hypertension:** every survey here measures BP on one occasion, not over repeated visits. The usual approach is to define hypertension as a measured BP of 140/90 or higher, or currently taking BP medication. Then estimate unawareness as the share of those people who were never told they have it.

## Next step
Start with NHANES 2017–2020 or 2021–2023 today. Register for ELSA and either CHARLS or LASI this week, since both are free or quick. The Harmonized HRS, ELSA, CHARLS and LASI files on g2aging.org save a lot of variable matching.

I checked access on 12 Nov 2026. Where something comes from memory, I say so.

## Shortlist

| # | Survey | Who measures BP | How you get it | Time | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NHANES** (US, all ages) | Certified examiners in a mobile exam centre | Free download, no login | minutes | today |
| 2 | **HRS** (US, 50+) | Trained interviewers in the home, not nurses | Free registration | minutes | HRS documentation, via search |
| 3 | **ELSA** (England, 50+) | Nurse visit | Free UK Data Service account | minutes–days | today |
| 4 | **CHARLS** (China, 45+) | Trained staff, 3 readings | Free registration and request | days | CHARLS documentation, via search |
| 5 | **LASI** (India, 45+) | Trained field staff | Request form with ID, reviewed in 24–48 h | days | today |
| 6 | **KNHANES** (Korea, all ages) | Examiners, NHANES-style | Free registration | days | papers' data statements |
| 7 | TILDA (Ireland, 50+) | Nurse health assessment | Application, non-commercial users only | weeks | today |
| 8 | CHMS (Canada) | Mobile clinic | Research Data Centre only | months | today |

## How to get each one

**1. NHANES.** Go to https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/ and download the public files for each cycle you want. For Aug 2021–Aug 2023 these are `DEMO_L`, `BPXO_L` and `BPQ_L`; merge them on `SEQN`.
- **BP:** three Omron readings taken by certified examiners after 5 minutes of seated rest, in the file `BPXO_L` (confirmed today).
- **Awareness:** `BPQ020`, "ever told by a doctor or other health professional that you had hypertension". `BPQ150` asks about current medication.
- **Weights:** use the exam (MEC) weights and the design variables (`SDMVPSU`, `SDMVSTRA`).
- **Caveat:** NHANES stopped mercury (auscultatory) measurements after 2017–18. If you pool cycles across that change, you need to handle the device switch.
- **Use:** the "Awareness of having hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia among US adults: NHANES 2011–2018" paper measures exactly your outcome.

**2. HRS.** Register for free at hrsdata.isr.umich.edu. Public data "only require you to register, log in, and access." Download the core health section (C) and physical measures section (I) for each wave, plus the tracker file for the weights. A cleaned, harmonised version is also on g2aging.org.
- **Who is measured:** since 2006 a random half of respondents gets the enhanced face-to-face interview each wave. That means each person is measured every 4 years.
- **Weights:** use the physical-measures weights.
- **2020 wave:** COVID disrupted the 2020 measurements, so skip it.
- **Caveat:** interviewers take the readings, not nurses. Say so in your methods.

**3. ELSA.** The ELSA site says "End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS" (confirmed today). Log in through your institution (UK Access Management Federation) or request a username if you're outside the UK. Then download the ELSA series, including the nurse files.
- **Nurse visits:** only every other wave (2, 4, 6, 8/9, from memory). COVID affected later waves.
- **Wave 0:** this is the Health Survey for England, which also has nurse-measured BP for all ages.

**4. CHARLS.** The documentation says the data are "freely available to all bona fide researchers." You register at charls.pku.edu.cn/en and submit a request. The site timed out from here, so check the current form yourself.
- **Waves:** use 2011–2018. The 2020 wave apparently had no physical exam, but I couldn't confirm that.
- **Use:** there is a CHARLS paper on hypertension awareness ([PMC6480849](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6480849/)).

**5. LASI.** Fill in the request form at https://www.iipsindia.ac.in/content/lasi-data and attach "a valid identity proof." Access is "only granted for legitimate academic research purposes", and IIPS reviews requests "within 24 to 48 hours" (all confirmed today). With about 73,000 respondents it gives a high-undiagnosed contrast to the US and England.

**6. KNHANES.** Register on knhanes.kdca.go.kr, accept the data use policy and download the raw files. The registration pages are mostly in Korean, and I couldn't confirm that foreign researchers can sign up.

## Not recommended
- **NHIS and BRFSS:** self-reported hypertension only, so they fail your main requirement.
- **SHARE:** as far as I recall, no BP measurement in the main survey.
- **MHAS (Mexico):** BP was measured only in a subsample, from memory, and I couldn't confirm the site.
- **TILDA and CHMS:** they fit the measurement requirement, but access is slower. TILDA needs an application and is for non-commercial users only. CHMS can only be used inside a Canadian Research Data Centre.

## Two things for your methods
- **Who did the measuring differs:** examiners (NHANES), nurses (ELSA) and trained interviewers or field staff (HRS, CHARLS, LASI). Say this in your methods.
- **A single visit overestimates hypertension:** every survey here measures BP on one occasion, not over repeated visits. The usual approach is to define hypertension as a measured BP of 140/90 or higher, or currently taking BP medication. Then estimate unawareness as the share of those people who were never told they have it.

## Next step
Start with NHANES 2017–2020 or 2021–2023 today. Register for ELSA and either CHARLS or LASI this week, since both are free or quick. The Harmonized HRS, ELSA, CHARLS and LASI files on g2aging.org save a lot of variable matching.

## What I couldn't check
The HRS site blocked automated access and the CHARLS site timed out, so their details come from their documentation. The registry searches were mostly noise; the useful candidates came from known studies and the literature.

Sources: [HRS New User Guide 2025](https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/new-user-guide/HRS-New-User-Guide-July-2025.pdf), [HRS 2006 Biomarker documentation](https://hrsonline.isr.umich.edu/modules/meta/bio2006/desc/biomkr06dd.pdf), [CHARLS baseline user guide](https://charls.charlsdata.com/Public/ashelf/public/uploads/document/2011-charls-wave1/application/CHARLS_nationalbaseline_users_guide.pdf), [Harmonized CHARLS](https://charls.charlsdata.com/Public/ashelf/public/uploads/document/harmonized_charls/application/Harmonized_CHARLS_D.pdf), [CHARLS awareness paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6480849/), [KNHANES profile](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4017741/), [KNHANES death-linkage paper](https://www.e-epih.org/journal/view.php?number=1269), [NHANES BPXO_L](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2021/DataFiles/BPXO_L.htm), [NHANES BPQ_L](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2021/DataFiles/BPQ_L.htm), [ELSA access](https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data), [LASI data](https://www.iipsindia.ac.in/content/lasi-data), [TILDA access](https://tilda.tcd.ie/data/accessing-data/)

The full shortlist is in an interactive page you can filter and export an access plan from: `/private/tmp/e-Ltg1Tb/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
For the US, use **NHANES**. For the comparison countries, I'd use **ELSA** (England) and either **CHARLS** (China) or **KNHANES** (South Korea). All four measure blood pressure as part of an exam and also ask whether a doctor ever told the respondent they have high blood pressure, so you can count people who meet the measured or medication definition but say they were never told.

## 1. NHANES (United States): your main survey

- **Why:** It's a nationally representative sample of all ages. Blood pressure is measured at a mobile exam centre (MEC), and CDC uses it for its own official figures on hypertension awareness. CDC Data Brief 511 reports these for Aug 2021–Aug 2023 (prevalence 47.7%), so you can check your numbers against it.
- **Files for the latest cycle (2021–2023, suffix `_L`):**
  - `BPXO_L`: three oscillometric readings (`BPXOSY1–3`, `BPXODI1–3`).
  - `BPQ_L`: the questionnaire with "ever told you had high blood pressure" and BP medication use.
  - `DEMO_L`: demographics, plus the survey design variables (`SDMVSTRA`, `SDMVPSU`) and the exam weight (`WTMEC2YR`).
- **Access:** None needed. The public XPT files download freely from the CDC NHANES site, with no registration.
- **Things to watch:**
  - From 2021 NHANES switched from auscultatory readings (`BPX` files in older cycles) to oscillometric ones. If you pool or trend across cycles, the protocol change matters.
  - Use the MEC exam weights, not the interview weights, and account for the survey design (stratum and PSU).
  - The 2017–March 2020 "pre-pandemic" file is the previous usable cycle.

## 2. ELSA (England, ages 50+): best match for older adults

- **Why:** It's a nationally representative sample of people aged 50 and over. A study nurse measures blood pressure at a home visit, following the Health Survey for England protocol. The core interview asks about doctor-diagnosed high blood pressure, and the nurse visit also records prescribed medications.
- **Which waves:** Nurse visits took place in waves 2, 4, 6, 8 and 9. In wave 9 (2018/19) only half the sample got a visit. Use the nurse-visit weights.
- **Access:**
  1. Register with the UK Data Service (study SN 5050).
  2. Accept the End User Licence, which is free for academic use.
  3. Download.

  I think the main nurse files are in the End User Licence release, but I couldn't confirm that. Check the access level on the SN 5050 catalogue page. Some variables are under Special Licence, which takes a short extra application.
- **Contact:** ELSAdata@natcen.ac.uk.

## 3. A third survey: choose one

- **CHARLS (China, ages 45+):** It's nationally representative. Trained field staff take three Omron readings rather than nurses, and you get the doctor-diagnosis question and medication use. It's widely used for studies of hypertension awareness. **Access:** register free on the CHARLS website (charls.pku.edu.cn), state how you'll use the data, and download once approved, usually within days.
- **KNHANES (South Korea, all ages):** It's built on the NHANES model, so it's the closest match in design: standardized measurement by trained examiners, plus a diagnosis question. **Access:** register free on the KDCA KNHANES site and submit a short data request. The documentation is partly in English.
- **Also possible:** LASI (India, 45+) has the same type of design as CHARLS. You request it through IIPS or the Gateway to Global Aging. HRS, the US sister study to ELSA, has had physical measures including BP, taken by interviewers in half the sample each wave since 2006, but NHANES is the stronger US source.

**Practical tip:** ELSA, CHARLS, LASI and HRS are harmonized by the **Gateway to Global Aging Data** (g2aging.org). It publishes consistent variable definitions across studies, which makes cross-country comparisons much easier to defend in a thesis.

**Methods points to settle early:**
- Pick one threshold, 140/90 or ACC/AHA 130/80, and apply it everywhere. Report the other one as a sensitivity analysis.
- Define "hypertensive" as measured high BP *or* taking BP medication.
- Average the readings the same way in every survey (e.g., the mean of the 2nd and 3rd).
- Note the measurement differences: nurse versus trained interviewer, and oscillometric versus auscultatory.

Sources:
- [NHANES 2021–2023 Examination Data](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/search/datapage.aspx?Component=Examination&Cycle=2021-2023)
- [NHANES 2021–2023 Questionnaire Data](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/search/datapage.aspx?Component=Questionnaire&Cycle=2021-2023)
- [NCHS Data Brief 511](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db511.htm)
- [ELSA Wave 4 Nurse Dataset User Guide](https://ifs.org.uk/sites/default/files/output_url_files/wave_4_nurse_dataset.pdf)
- [ELSA Wave 9 Technical Report (UKDS SN 5050)](https://doc.ukdataservice.ac.uk/doc/5050/mrdoc/pdf/5050_elsa_w9_technical_report_v3.pdf)
- [UKDS ELSA update](https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/app/uploads/pacchiotti.pdf)
- [ELSA on Atlas of Longitudinal Datasets](https://atlaslongitudinaldatasets.ac.uk/datasets/elsa)
