## Details and how to get each one
1. **NHANES 2011–2014** ([PAXMIN_G docs](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2011/DataFiles/PAXMIN_G.htm), [mortality linkage](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/linked-data/mortality-files/)).
   - **Data:** about 99% of monitors were on the non-dominant wrist. Files include a minute-by-minute wake/sleep/non-wear prediction (`PAXPREDM`), and the raw 80 Hz data is about 1 TB compressed.
   - **Get it:** download the accelerometer files and the public-use mortality file directly. The public mortality file comes from an earlier linkage and has altered details. Follow-up to 2022 and the Medicare linkage are only in restricted files at an NCHS Research Data Center, which needs a project application.
   - **Extra files:** activity counts and step counts per minute for all 14,693 wearers are on [PhysioNet](https://physionet.org/content/minute-level-step-count-nhanes/1.0.2/) (CC0, open).
   - **Example paper:** an [activity fragmentation and mortality study](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-29778-9) (2026).
   - Use the survey weights.
2. **All of Us** ([access tiers](https://www.researchallofus.org/data-tools/data-access/)).
   - **Get it:** your institution's signing official signs the DURA (many US universities already have). You then register, verify your identity and complete the research conduct training. Controlled-tier data (including deaths) needs extra training.
   - **Caveats:** Fitbit gives proprietary summaries, not raw acceleration, so comparing with raw-signal wrist studies is limited. People who share Fitbit data are a self-selected group. Analysis is cloud-only.
   - **Example papers:** [Nature Medicine 2022 on step counts and chronic disease](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-022-02012-w), and [a 2026 Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes paper on sleep](https://doi.org/10.1161/circoutcomes.126.014445).
3. **UK Biobank** ([apply](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/apply-for-access/), [fees](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/)).
   - **Why it matters:** this is the reference dataset most other wrist studies use, so it's the best one for comparability.
   - **Status:** its analysis platform was suspended on 23 April 2026. Reopening reportedly waits on government approval, exporting results files will at first be restricted, and new GP data is being withheld for now.
   - **Get it:** register in the Access Management System now and watch the UK Biobank Community site for the reopening date.
   - **Example papers:** [Doherty 2017](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0169649) and [activity and 697 diseases (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-022-00676-9).
4. **Whitehall II** ([data-sharing FAQ](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/brain-sciences/psychiatry/our-research/mental-health-older-people/whitehall-ii/data-sharing/data-sharing-faq)).
   - **Get it:** apply through the DPUK portal. A committee meets monthly, then you sign a data sharing agreement. Sources disagree on whether the £500+VAT fee still applies, so ask whitehall2@ucl.ac.uk.
   - **Caveats:** analysis is probably inside DPUK's secure environment. Participants were aged about 60–83 and mostly white.
   - **Example paper:** [epoch choice and mortality (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-30237-5).
5. **China Kadoorie Biobank** ([access policy](https://www.ckbiobank.org/data-access/data-2)).
   - **Why it's useful:** it uses the same AX3 wrist device as UK Biobank.
   - **Unconfirmed:** CKB researchers get exclusive use before data is released, and I couldn't confirm whether the accelerometer data is out yet. Check the data overview page.
   - **Description paper:** [IJBNPA 2023](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-023-01537-8).
6. **MrOS / SOF** ([MrOS Online](https://mrosonline.ucsf.edu/)).
   - **Good for:** sleep and rest-activity rhythms.
   - **Limits:** older-device counts aren't comparable with raw-signal metrics. The NSRR copy of MrOS has no actigraphy, so use MrOS Online.
   - **Example paper:** [rest/activity rhythms and mortality (2010)](https://doi.org/10.3109/07420520903419157).

## Known, not confirmed
- **Pelotas 1982/1993 birth cohorts** (GENEActiv wrist, several thousand young adults) and the **Rotterdam Study** (GENEActiv wrist) may fit, but I didn't check their size, outcome linkage or access.
- **Websites I couldn't read directly:** UK Biobank, UCL, CKB and sleepdata.org blocked automated requests. Their terms above come from search-engine snippets of their official pages, so confirm them in a browser.

## Not recommended
- **MESA Sleep:** wrist Actiwatch with confirmed cardiovascular events, but only 2,237 people. Good for replication.
- **HCHS/SOL Sueño:** about 2,200 people with wrist devices; the main study measured activity at the hip.
- **Wrong body placement (from memory):** NHANES 2003–06, WHI OPACH, the Women's Health Study, CARDIA and NAKO used hip devices; HUNT4 and the 1970 British Cohort used thigh or back devices.

## Next step
Download NHANES and the public mortality file now to build your pipeline (e.g. GGIR for raw data). In parallel, check your university's All of Us DURA status and send a Whitehall II application. If you want a US hospital-outcome analysis, plan an NCHS Research Data Center proposal for the Medicare linkage. Register with UK Biobank so you're ready when it reopens.

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
I found eight datasets worth considering. The one most wrist studies compare against, **UK Biobank, is not taking new applications right now**. **NHANES 2011–2014 is the one you can start on today**, and **All of Us** is likely the fastest route to records-linked data for a US university.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** a wrist-worn device; several days or more of everyday wear; a few thousand adults or more; linked outcomes (hospital records, diagnoses or deaths).
- **Nice to have:** raw or minute-level signal, so you can process it the same way as other wrist studies.
- **Assumed:** non-US cohorts are fine, and waiting weeks to months for approval is acceptable.

## Shortlist (checked 12 Nov 2026)
| # | Dataset | Access | Wrist device / size | Outcomes | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES 2011–14 + Linked Mortality Files | Direct download; minutes | ActiGraph GT3X+, 9 days, ~12,600–14,700 | Deaths only (to 2019 public; to 2022 restricted) | today |
| 2 | UK Biobank accelerometer sub-study | Application + fee; **new applications paused** | Axivity AX3, 7 days, ~100k | Hospital records, deaths, cancer | today (web search) |
| 3 | All of Us (Fitbit + health records) | Institutional agreement + training; days | Fitbit, often months, 12.8k in 2022 (more now) | Health-record diagnoses | today |
| 4 | Whitehall II (GENEActiv) | Application via Dementias Platform UK; weeks | GENEActiv, 9 days, 4,204 | Deaths; hospital records from memory | today (web search) |
| 5 | China Kadoorie Biobank, 3rd resurvey | Application; months; release status unclear | Axivity AX3, 7 days, ~20,400 | Hospital insurance and death registries (from memory); short follow-up | today (web search) |
| 6 | MrOS (older men) | Free registration + online agreement; days | Wrist actigraph, ~5 nights, 3,135 | Reviewed deaths and heart events, ~15 yrs | today (web search) |
| 7 | MESA Sleep | Agreement + ethics approval (IRB); weeks | Actiwatch, 7 days, 2,237 | Heart events via a separate request | today (web search) |
| 8 | Rush Memory and Aging Project | Data request; weeks | Actical, up to 10 days, repeated, ~1,000+ | Deaths, dementia, autopsy | today (web search) |

"Today" means I confirmed the page with the checking tool. "Today (web search)" means the site blocked automated checks (UK Biobank, UCL, CKB, UCSF, sleepdata.org and Rush all did), so those facts come from web search results today, not from the site itself.

## Details and access steps
**1. NHANES 2011–2014.** Participants wore an ActiGraph on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days, and minute-level files (in MIMS units) are released.
- **Access:** download the activity files for the 2011–12 and 2013–14 cycles, then the public mortality files from the [CDC linked-data page](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm). No application.
- **Limits:** the public files end follow-up on 31 Dec 2019, and CDC alters follow-up time or cause of death for a few records to protect privacy. Follow-up to 2022 is only available as restricted files through an NCHS Research Data Center, which takes months.
- **Outcomes:** deaths only, no hospital records.
- **Example paper:** [PMC11402588](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/).

**2. UK Biobank.** Still the best match on paper: about 100k adults, raw 100 Hz signal, and linked hospital, cancer and death records.
- **Status:** its FAQ (updated 22 Oct 2026) says "We are not currently accepting applications for new research projects", with reopening planned for late 2026. This follows a [data leak in 2026](https://www.the-scientist.com/uk-biobank-to-restore-access-months-after-massive-data-leak-75197).
- **Fees when it reopens:** Tier 1 is £3,000 for 3 years (£500 for students, who must apply with their supervisor). See the [fees page](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/).
- **Where you analyse:** only on its cloud platform (UKB-RAP), with compute billed separately. Some new linked health data is being held back until government data providers sign off.
- **Plan for now:** register on its application system and prepare your proposal.
- **Example paper:** [10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213).

**3. All of Us.**
- **Access:** your university must have signed a Data Use and Registration Agreement (most large US universities have). You then register on the [Researcher Workbench](https://www.researchallofus.org/data-tools/workbench/), verify your identity and complete training. The Controlled Tier, which has real event dates, needs an amended agreement and extra training.
- **Rules:** you work only in their cloud workbench and may not link records to outside data.
- **Caveat for comparability:** this is consumer-tracker output (steps, heart rate, sleep stages), not raw acceleration. People who already own a Fitbit are also not a random sample.
- **Recent papers:** many on sleep, activity and disease.

**4. Whitehall II.** About 4,200 participants wore a GENEActiv on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days in 2012–13.
- **Access:** apply through the [DPUK portal](https://portal.dementiasplatform.uk/data/cohort-data-availability/). You choose variables, the Whitehall committee reviews the request, you sign an access agreement and you analyse in a secure remote environment.
- **To ask:** whether the raw device files are available (whitehall2@ucl.ac.uk).

**5. China Kadoorie Biobank.** The same device as UK Biobank, worn by about 20,000 adults in 2020–21 ([Chen et al. 2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12966-023-01537-8)).
- **Status:** I could not confirm whether the accelerometer data has been released to researchers through the CKB Data Access System yet.
- **Limit:** follow-up is still short.

**6. MrOS.** Free registration and an online data-use agreement on MrOS Online. It has actigraphy from the sleep visit (n=3,135) and mortality with more than half of participants deceased. See this [mortality paper](https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/45/4/zsac015/6509372). The sister study of older women, SOF (about 3,000), is requested through SOF Online, and its access terms are not confirmed.

**7. MESA Sleep.** Raw actigraphy is on the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR), which needs a data-use agreement and ethics approval (IRB). Heart events must be requested separately from BioLINCC or the MESA Coordinating Center.

**8. Rush Memory and Aging Project.** Request through the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center (RADC) Research Resource Sharing Hub. It is smaller than your target, but people wore the device repeatedly over years.

## Known, not confirmed
- The device MrOS used (from memory: SleepWatch-O, a wrist actigraph), and whether raw epochs are available.
- Whitehall II's hospital-record linkage (from memory).
- Two smaller US cohorts I did not check: the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (wrist ActiGraph/GENEActiv, roughly 1,000 people, application at blsa.nih.gov) and the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF).

## Not recommended
These wore the device on the hip or thigh, which fails your wrist requirement:
- NHANES 2003–06, the Women's Health Study and the WHI OPACH study (hip)
- HUNT4 (thigh and lower back)
- REGARDS, Tromsø 7 and the German National Cohort (hip, from memory)
- 1970 British Cohort Study (thigh)

These are wrist-based but probably fall short:
- HCHS/SOL Sueño: about 1,900 participants on NSRR, and published work so far does not follow people over time.
- Rotterdam Study (GENEActiv): about 1,200–1,400 people, requested by email.

## What I could not find
No openly downloadable wrist dataset that is also linked to hospital records. NHANES has deaths only.

## Next step
1. Start on NHANES now.
2. Check whether your university has an All of Us agreement, and register.
3. Draft a UK Biobank application for when it reopens.
4. Email the Whitehall II team about the raw device files.

Pooling NHANES or All of Us with UK Biobank and Whitehall II would give you external validation on different wrist devices.

I've saved an interactive version of this shortlist, where you can filter, compare datasets and export an access plan: `/private/tmp/e-Dth5Qj/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`

| # | Dataset | Access | Wrist device / size | Outcomes | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES 2011–14 + Linked Mortality Files | Direct download; minutes | ActiGraph GT3X+, 9 days, ~12,600–14,700 | Deaths only (to 2019 public; to 2022 restricted) | today |
| 2 | UK Biobank accelerometer sub-study | Application + fee; **new applications paused** | Axivity AX3, 7 days, ~100k | Hospital records, deaths, cancer | today (web search) |
| 3 | All of Us (Fitbit + health records) | Institutional agreement + training; days | Fitbit, often months, 12.8k in 2022 (more now) | Health-record diagnoses | today |
| 4 | Whitehall II (GENEActiv) | Application via Dementias Platform UK; weeks | GENEActiv, 9 days, 4,204 | Deaths; hospital records from memory | today (web search) |
| 5 | China Kadoorie Biobank, 3rd resurvey | Application; months; release status unclear | Axivity AX3, 7 days, ~20,400 | Hospital insurance and death registries (from memory); short follow-up | today (web search) |
| 6 | MrOS (older men) | Free registration + online agreement; days | Wrist actigraph, ~5 nights, 3,135 | Reviewed deaths and heart events, ~15 yrs | today (web search) |
| 7 | MESA Sleep | Agreement + ethics approval (IRB); weeks | Actiwatch, 7 days, 2,237 | Heart events via a separate request | today (web search) |
| 8 | Rush Memory and Aging Project | Data request; weeks | Actical, up to 10 days, repeated, ~1,000+ | Deaths, dementia, autopsy | today (web search) |

"Today" means I confirmed the page with the checking tool. "Today (web search)" means the site blocked automated checks (UK Biobank, UCL, CKB, UCSF, sleepdata.org and Rush all did), so those facts come from web search results today, not from the site itself.

## Details and access steps
**1. NHANES 2011–2014.** Participants wore an ActiGraph on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days, and minute-level files (in MIMS units) are released.
- **Access:** download the activity files for the 2011–12 and 2013–14 cycles, then the public mortality files from the [CDC linked-data page](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm). No application.
- **Limits:** the public files end follow-up on 31 Dec 2019, and CDC alters follow-up time or cause of death for a few records to protect privacy. Follow-up to 2022 is only available as restricted files through an NCHS Research Data Center, which takes months.
- **Outcomes:** deaths only, no hospital records.
- **Example paper:** [PMC11402588](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/).

**2. UK Biobank.** Still the best match on paper: about 100k adults, raw 100 Hz signal, and linked hospital, cancer and death records.
- **Status:** its FAQ (updated 22 Oct 2026) says "We are not currently accepting applications for new research projects", with reopening planned for late 2026. This follows a [data leak in 2026](https://www.the-scientist.com/uk-biobank-to-restore-access-months-after-massive-data-leak-75197).
- **Fees when it reopens:** Tier 1 is £3,000 for 3 years (£500 for students, who must apply with their supervisor). See the [fees page](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/).
- **Where you analyse:** only on its cloud platform (UKB-RAP), with compute billed separately. Some new linked health data is being held back until government data providers sign off.
- **Plan for now:** register on its application system and prepare your proposal.
- **Example paper:** [10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213).

**3. All of Us.**
- **Access:** your university must have signed a Data Use and Registration Agreement (most large US universities have). You then register on the [Researcher Workbench](https://www.researchallofus.org/data-tools/workbench/), verify your identity and complete training. The Controlled Tier, which has real event dates, needs an amended agreement and extra training.
- **Rules:** you work only in their cloud workbench and may not link records to outside data.
- **Caveat for comparability:** this is consumer-tracker output (steps, heart rate, sleep stages), not raw acceleration. People who already own a Fitbit are also not a random sample.
- **Recent papers:** many on sleep, activity and disease.

**4. Whitehall II.** About 4,200 participants wore a GENEActiv on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days in 2012–13.
- **Access:** apply through the [DPUK portal](https://portal.dementiasplatform.uk/data/cohort-data-availability/). You choose variables, the Whitehall committee reviews the request, you sign an access agreement and you analyse in a secure remote environment.
- **To ask:** whether the raw device files are available (whitehall2@ucl.ac.uk).

**5. China Kadoorie Biobank.** The same device as UK Biobank, worn by about 20,000 adults in 2020–21 ([Chen et al. 2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12966-023-01537-8)).
- **Status:** I could not confirm whether the accelerometer data has been released to researchers through the CKB Data Access System yet.
- **Limit:** follow-up is still short.

**6. MrOS.** Free registration and an online data-use agreement on MrOS Online. It has actigraphy from the sleep visit (n=3,135) and mortality with more than half of participants deceased. See this [mortality paper](https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/45/4/zsac015/6509372). The sister study of older women, SOF (about 3,000), is requested through SOF Online, and its access terms are not confirmed.

**7. MESA Sleep.** Raw actigraphy is on the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR), which needs a data-use agreement and ethics approval (IRB). Heart events must be requested separately from BioLINCC or the MESA Coordinating Center.

**8. Rush Memory and Aging Project.** Request through the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center (RADC) Research Resource Sharing Hub. It is smaller than your target, but people wore the device repeatedly over years.

## Known, not confirmed
- The device MrOS used (from memory: SleepWatch-O, a wrist actigraph), and whether raw epochs are available.
- Whitehall II's hospital-record linkage (from memory).
- Two smaller US cohorts I did not check: the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (wrist ActiGraph/GENEActiv, roughly 1,000 people, application at blsa.nih.gov) and the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF).

## Not recommended
These wore the device on the hip or thigh, which fails your wrist requirement:
- NHANES 2003–06, the Women's Health Study and the WHI OPACH study (hip)
- HUNT4 (thigh and lower back)
- REGARDS, Tromsø 7 and the German National Cohort (hip, from memory)
- 1970 British Cohort Study (thigh)

These are wrist-based but probably fall short:
- HCHS/SOL Sueño: about 1,900 participants on NSRR, and published work so far does not follow people over time.
- Rotterdam Study (GENEActiv): about 1,200–1,400 people, requested by email.

## What I could not find
No openly downloadable wrist dataset that is also linked to hospital records. NHANES has deaths only.

## Next step
1. Start on NHANES now.
2. Check whether your university has an All of Us agreement, and register.
3. Draft a UK Biobank application for when it reopens.
4. Email the Whitehall II team about the raw device files.

Pooling NHANES or All of Us with UK Biobank and Whitehall II would give you external validation on different wrist devices.

I found eight datasets worth considering. The one most wrist studies compare against, **UK Biobank, is not taking new applications right now**. **NHANES 2011–2014 is the one you can start on today**, and **All of Us** is likely the fastest route to records-linked data for a US university.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** a wrist-worn device; several days or more of everyday wear; a few thousand adults or more; linked outcomes (hospital records, diagnoses or deaths).
- **Nice to have:** raw or minute-level signal, so you can process it the same way as other wrist studies.
- **Assumed:** non-US cohorts are fine, and waiting weeks to months for approval is acceptable.

## Shortlist (checked 12 Nov 2026)
| # | Dataset | Access | Wrist device / size | Outcomes | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES 2011–14 + Linked Mortality Files | Direct download; minutes | ActiGraph GT3X+, 9 days, ~12,600–14,700 | Deaths only (to 2019 public; to 2022 restricted) | today |
| 2 | UK Biobank accelerometer sub-study | Application + fee; **new applications paused** | Axivity AX3, 7 days, ~100k | Hospital records, deaths, cancer | today (web search) |
| 3 | All of Us (Fitbit + health records) | Institutional agreement + training; days | Fitbit, often months, 12.8k in 2022 (more now) | Health-record diagnoses | today |
| 4 | Whitehall II (GENEActiv) | Application via Dementias Platform UK; weeks | GENEActiv, 9 days, 4,204 | Deaths; hospital records from memory | today (web search) |
| 5 | China Kadoorie Biobank, 3rd resurvey | Application; months; release status unclear | Axivity AX3, 7 days, ~20,400 | Hospital insurance and death registries (from memory); short follow-up | today (web search) |
| 6 | MrOS (older men) | Free registration + online agreement; days | Wrist actigraph, ~5 nights, 3,135 | Reviewed deaths and heart events, ~15 yrs | today (web search) |
| 7 | MESA Sleep | Agreement + ethics approval (IRB); weeks | Actiwatch, 7 days, 2,237 | Heart events via a separate request | today (web search) |
| 8 | Rush Memory and Aging Project | Data request; weeks | Actical, up to 10 days, repeated, ~1,000+ | Deaths, dementia, autopsy | today (web search) |

"Today" means I confirmed the page with the checking tool. "Today (web search)" means the site blocked automated checks (UK Biobank, UCL, CKB, UCSF, sleepdata.org and Rush all did), so those facts come from web search results today, not from the site itself.

## Details and access steps
**1. NHANES 2011–2014.** Participants wore an ActiGraph on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days, and minute-level files (in MIMS units) are released.
- **Access:** download the activity files for the 2011–12 and 2013–14 cycles, then the public mortality files from the [CDC linked-data page](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm). No application.
- **Limits:** the public files end follow-up on 31 Dec 2019, and CDC alters follow-up time or cause of death for a few records to protect privacy. Follow-up to 2022 is only available as restricted files through an NCHS Research Data Center, which takes months.
- **Outcomes:** deaths only, no hospital records.
- **Example paper:** [PMC11402588](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/).

**2. UK Biobank.** Still the best match on paper: about 100k adults, raw 100 Hz signal, and linked hospital, cancer and death records.
- **Status:** its FAQ (updated 22 Oct 2026) says "We are not currently accepting applications for new research projects", with reopening planned for late 2026. This follows a [data leak in 2026](https://www.the-scientist.com/uk-biobank-to-restore-access-months-after-massive-data-leak-75197).
- **Fees when it reopens:** Tier 1 is £3,000 for 3 years (£500 for students, who must apply with their supervisor). See the [fees page](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/).
- **Where you analyse:** only on its cloud platform (UKB-RAP), with compute billed separately. Some new linked health data is being held back until government data providers sign off.
- **Plan for now:** register on its application system and prepare your proposal.
- **Example paper:** [10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213).

**3. All of Us.**
- **Access:** your university must have signed a Data Use and Registration Agreement (most large US universities have). You then register on the [Researcher Workbench](https://www.researchallofus.org/data-tools/workbench/), verify your identity and complete training. The Controlled Tier, which has real event dates, needs an amended agreement and extra training.
- **Rules:** you work only in their cloud workbench and may not link records to outside data.
- **Caveat for comparability:** this is consumer-tracker output (steps, heart rate, sleep stages), not raw acceleration. People who already own a Fitbit are also not a random sample.
- **Recent papers:** many on sleep, activity and disease.

**4. Whitehall II.** About 4,200 participants wore a GENEActiv on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days in 2012–13.
- **Access:** apply through the [DPUK portal](https://portal.dementiasplatform.uk/data/cohort-data-availability/). You choose variables, the Whitehall committee reviews the request, you sign an access agreement and you analyse in a secure remote environment.
- **To ask:** whether the raw device files are available (whitehall2@ucl.ac.uk).

**5. China Kadoorie Biobank.** The same device as UK Biobank, worn by about 20,000 adults in 2020–21 ([Chen et al. 2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12966-023-01537-8)).
- **Status:** I could not confirm whether the accelerometer data has been released to researchers through the CKB Data Access System yet.
- **Limit:** follow-up is still short.

**6. MrOS.** Free registration and an online data-use agreement on MrOS Online. It has actigraphy from the sleep visit (n=3,135) and mortality with more than half of participants deceased. See this [mortality paper](https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/45/4/zsac015/6509372). The sister study of older women, SOF (about 3,000), is requested through SOF Online, and its access terms are not confirmed.

**7. MESA Sleep.** Raw actigraphy is on the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR), which needs a data-use agreement and ethics approval (IRB). Heart events must be requested separately from BioLINCC or the MESA Coordinating Center.

**8. Rush Memory and Aging Project.** Request through the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center (RADC) Research Resource Sharing Hub. It is smaller than your target, but people wore the device repeatedly over years.

## Known, not confirmed
- The device MrOS used (from memory: SleepWatch-O, a wrist actigraph), and whether raw epochs are available.
- Whitehall II's hospital-record linkage (from memory).
- Two smaller US cohorts I did not check: the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (wrist ActiGraph/GENEActiv, roughly 1,000 people, application at blsa.nih.gov) and the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF).

## Not recommended
These wore the device on the hip or thigh, which fails your wrist requirement:
- NHANES 2003–06, the Women's Health Study and the WHI OPACH study (hip)
- HUNT4 (thigh and lower back)
- REGARDS, Tromsø 7 and the German National Cohort (hip, from memory)
- 1970 British Cohort Study (thigh)

These are wrist-based but probably fall short:
- HCHS/SOL Sueño: about 1,900 participants on NSRR, and published work so far does not follow people over time.
- Rotterdam Study (GENEActiv): about 1,200–1,400 people, requested by email.

## What I could not find
No openly downloadable wrist dataset that is also linked to hospital records. NHANES has deaths only.

## Next step
1. Start on NHANES now.
2. Check whether your university has an All of Us agreement, and register.
3. Draft a UK Biobank application for when it reopens.
4. Email the Whitehall II team about the raw device files.

Pooling NHANES or All of Us with UK Biobank and Whitehall II would give you external validation on different wrist devices.

See this [mortality paper](https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/45/4/zsac015/6509372). The sister study of older women, SOF (about 3,000), is requested through SOF Online, and its access terms are not confirmed.

**7. MESA Sleep.** Raw actigraphy is on the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR), which needs a data-use agreement and ethics approval (IRB). Heart events must be requested separately from BioLINCC or the MESA Coordinating Center.

**8. Rush Memory and Aging Project.** Request through the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center (RADC) Research Resource Sharing Hub. It is smaller than your target, but people wore the device repeatedly over years.

## Known, not confirmed
- The device MrOS used (from memory: SleepWatch-O, a wrist actigraph), and whether raw epochs are available.
- Whitehall II's hospital-record linkage (from memory).
- Two smaller US cohorts I did not check: the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (wrist ActiGraph/GENEActiv, roughly 1,000 people, application at blsa.nih.gov) and the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF).

## Not recommended
These wore the device on the hip or thigh, which fails your wrist requirement:
- NHANES 2003–06, the Women's Health Study and the WHI OPACH study (hip)
- HUNT4 (thigh and lower back)
- REGARDS, Tromsø 7 and the German National Cohort (hip, from memory)
- 1970 British Cohort Study (thigh)

These are wrist-based but probably fall short:
- HCHS/SOL Sueño: about 1,900 participants on NSRR, and published work so far does not follow people over time.
- Rotterdam Study (GENEActiv): about 1,200–1,400 people, requested by email.

## What I could not find
No openly downloadable wrist dataset that is also linked to hospital records. NHANES has deaths only.

## Next step
1. Start on NHANES now.
2. Check whether your university has an All of Us agreement, and register.
3. Draft a UK Biobank application for when it reopens.
4. Email the Whitehall II team about the raw device files.

Pooling NHANES or All of Us with UK Biobank and Whitehall II would give you external validation on different wrist devices.

I found eight datasets worth considering. The one most wrist studies compare against, **UK Biobank, is not taking new applications right now**. **NHANES 2011–2014 is the one you can start on today**, and **All of Us** is likely the fastest route to records-linked data for a US university.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** a wrist-worn device; several days or more of everyday wear; a few thousand adults or more; linked outcomes (hospital records, diagnoses or deaths).
- **Nice to have:** raw or minute-level signal, so you can process it the same way as other wrist studies.
- **Assumed:** non-US cohorts are fine, and waiting weeks to months for approval is acceptable.

## Shortlist (checked 12 Nov 2026)
| # | Dataset | Access | Wrist device / size | Outcomes | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES 2011–14 + Linked Mortality Files | Direct download; minutes | ActiGraph GT3X+, 9 days, ~12,600–14,700 | Deaths only (to 2019 public; to 2022 restricted) | today |
| 2 | UK Biobank accelerometer sub-study | Application + fee; **new applications paused** | Axivity AX3, 7 days, ~100k | Hospital records, deaths, cancer | today (web search) |
| 3 | All of Us (Fitbit + health records) | Institutional agreement + training; days | Fitbit, often months, 12.8k in 2022 (more now) | Health-record diagnoses | today |
| 4 | Whitehall II (GENEActiv) | Application via Dementias Platform UK; weeks | GENEActiv, 9 days, 4,204 | Deaths; hospital records from memory | today (web search) |
| 5 | China Kadoorie Biobank, 3rd resurvey | Application; months; release status unclear | Axivity AX3, 7 days, ~20,400 | Hospital insurance and death registries (from memory); short follow-up | today (web search) |
| 6 | MrOS (older men) | Free registration + online agreement; days | Wrist actigraph, ~5 nights, 3,135 | Reviewed deaths and heart events, ~15 yrs | today (web search) |
| 7 | MESA Sleep | Agreement + ethics approval (IRB); weeks | Actiwatch, 7 days, 2,237 | Heart events via a separate request | today (web search) |
| 8 | Rush Memory and Aging Project | Data request; weeks | Actical, up to 10 days, repeated, ~1,000+ | Deaths, dementia, autopsy | today (web search) |

"Today" means I confirmed the page with the checking tool. "Today (web search)" means the site blocked automated checks (UK Biobank, UCL, CKB, UCSF, sleepdata.org and Rush all did), so those facts come from web search results today, not from the site itself.

## Details and access steps
**1. NHANES 2011–2014.** Participants wore an ActiGraph on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days, and minute-level files (in MIMS units) are released.
- **Access:** download the activity files for the 2011–12 and 2013–14 cycles, then the public mortality files from the [CDC linked-data page](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm). No application.
- **Limits:** the public files end follow-up on 31 Dec 2019, and CDC alters follow-up time or cause of death for a few records to protect privacy. Follow-up to 2022 is only available as restricted files through an NCHS Research Data Center, which takes months.
- **Outcomes:** deaths only, no hospital records.
- **Example paper:** [PMC11402588](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/).

**2. UK Biobank.** Still the best match on paper: about 100k adults, raw 100 Hz signal, and linked hospital, cancer and death records.
- **Status:** its FAQ (updated 22 Oct 2026) says "We are not currently accepting applications for new research projects", with reopening planned for late 2026. This follows a [data leak in 2026](https://www.the-scientist.com/uk-biobank-to-restore-access-months-after-massive-data-leak-75197).
- **Fees when it reopens:** Tier 1 is £3,000 for 3 years (£500 for students, who must apply with their supervisor). See the [fees page](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/).
- **Where you analyse:** only on its cloud platform (UKB-RAP), with compute billed separately. Some new linked health data is being held back until government data providers sign off.
- **Plan for now:** register on its application system and prepare your proposal.
- **Example paper:** [10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213).

**3. All of Us.**
- **Access:** your university must have signed a Data Use and Registration Agreement (most large US universities have). You then register on the [Researcher Workbench](https://www.researchallofus.org/data-tools/workbench/), verify your identity and complete training. The Controlled Tier, which has real event dates, needs an amended agreement and extra training.
- **Rules:** you work only in their cloud workbench and may not link records to outside data.
- **Caveat for comparability:** this is consumer-tracker output (steps, heart rate, sleep stages), not raw acceleration. People who already own a Fitbit are also not a random sample.
- **Recent papers:** many on sleep, activity and disease.

**4. Whitehall II.** About 4,200 participants wore a GENEActiv on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days in 2012–13.
- **Access:** apply through the [DPUK portal](https://portal.dementiasplatform.uk/data/cohort-data-availability/). You choose variables, the Whitehall committee reviews the request, you sign an access agreement and you analyse in a secure remote environment.
- **To ask:** whether the raw device files are available (whitehall2@ucl.ac.uk).

**5. China Kadoorie Biobank.** The same device as UK Biobank, worn by about 20,000 adults in 2020–21 ([Chen et al. 2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12966-023-01537-8)).
- **Status:** I could not confirm whether the accelerometer data has been released to researchers through the CKB Data Access System yet.
- **Limit:** follow-up is still short.

**6. MrOS.** Free registration and an online data-use agreement on MrOS Online. It has actigraphy from the sleep visit (n=3,135) and mortality with more than half of participants deceased. See this [mortality paper](https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/45/4/zsac015/6509372). The sister study of older women, SOF (about 3,000), is requested through SOF Online, and its access terms are not confirmed.

**7. MESA Sleep.** Raw actigraphy is on the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR), which needs a data-use agreement and ethics approval (IRB). Heart events must be requested separately from BioLINCC or the MESA Coordinating Center.

**8. Rush Memory and Aging Project.** Request through the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center (RADC) Research Resource Sharing Hub. It is smaller than your target, but people wore the device repeatedly over years.

## Known, not confirmed
- The device MrOS used (from memory: SleepWatch-O, a wrist actigraph), and whether raw epochs are available.
- Whitehall II's hospital-record linkage (from memory).
- Two smaller US cohorts I did not check: the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (wrist ActiGraph/GENEActiv, roughly 1,000 people, application at blsa.nih.gov) and the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF).

## Not recommended
These wore the device on the hip or thigh, which fails your wrist requirement:

- HUNT4 (thigh and lower back)
- REGARDS, Tromsø 7 and the German National Cohort (hip, from memory)
- 1970 British Cohort Study (thigh)

These are wrist-based but probably fall short:
- HCHS/SOL Sueño: about 1,900 participants on NSRR, and published work so far does not follow people over time.
- Rotterdam Study (GENEActiv): about 1,200–1,400 people, requested by email.

## What I could not find
No openly downloadable wrist dataset that is also linked to hospital records. NHANES has deaths only.

## Next step
1. Start on NHANES now.
2. Check whether your university has an All of Us agreement, and register.
3. Draft a UK Biobank application for when it reopens.
4. Email the Whitehall II team about the raw device files.

Pooling NHANES or All of Us with UK Biobank and Whitehall II would give you external validation on different wrist devices.

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
For a US-based study of wrist accelerometry predicting later outcomes, the three main options are **UK Biobank** (largest, best outcome linkage), **NHANES 2011–2014** (free, US, linked to deaths) and **All of Us** (US, Fitbit plus medical records). After those come several smaller cohorts that are still useful. I wrote this from what I already know and didn't look anything up during this session. Treat fees, sample sizes and follow-up end dates as approximate, and check them on each study's site before you plan around them.

## Main options

### 1. UK Biobank accelerometer sub-study (best overall fit)
- **Device and wear:** Axivity AX3 on the **dominant wrist**, about 7 days of continuous wear, collected 2013–2015. Roughly 100,000 participants aged about 43–79. Raw 100 Hz data and processed summaries (activity, sleep and sedentary measures, ENMO) are both available. A few thousand participants also did repeat wears across seasons.
- **Outcomes:** linked hospital records for England, Scotland and Wales, national death and cancer registries, and GP records for part of the cohort. That gives roughly 8–10 years of follow-up after the wear week, so even fairly uncommon diseases have enough cases to study. This is the reference dataset most wrist-accelerometry outcome papers use.
- **Access:**
  1. Register yourself and your university on UK Biobank's Access Management System.
  2. Submit a research proposal. Approval usually takes weeks.
  3. Your institution signs a Material Transfer Agreement.
  4. Pay a tiered access fee, typically a few thousand pounds for three years, with reductions for students and early-career researchers.
- **Practical point:** analysis now happens only on UK Biobank's cloud platform (the Research Analysis Platform on DNAnexus). Data can't be downloaded, so budget for compute and storage, which matters if you reprocess the raw files. US universities apply routinely.

### 2. NHANES 2011–2014 (free, nationally representative US sample)
- **Device and wear:** ActiGraph GT3X+ on the **non-dominant wrist**, 7 days around the clock. About 7,000–9,000 adults have valid data. Minute-level summaries (in MIMS units) are public, and NCHS has also released the raw 80 Hz files.
- **Outcomes:** the public-use Linked Mortality Files connect participants to the National Death Index, including underlying cause of death. The most recent public follow-up I know of runs to the end of 2019, so check whether a newer one has been released. Medicare claims and the more detailed restricted mortality file are only available through an NCHS Research Data Center.
- **Access:** the public data has no application at all; you just download it. The Research Data Center route requires a proposal, a fee and work in a secure enclave.
- **Limitations:** mortality is the only outcome without the Research Data Center, follow-up is shorter, and the number of deaths is moderate. Use the survey weights. The older NHANES 2003–2006 accelerometer data was worn on the **hip**, so don't combine it with the wrist data.

### 3. All of Us Research Program (US, consumer trackers plus medical records)
- **Device and wear:** participants' own Fitbits (wrist-worn), plus devices the program has handed out. Tens of thousands of people have Fitbit data, often covering months to years. Measures include steps, heart rate, sleep stages and active minutes.
- **Outcomes:** electronic health records (diagnoses, procedures, labs) and surveys. Some mortality data exists. Check what the current release includes.
- **Access:**
  1. Your university signs a Data Use and Registration Agreement (many already have one).
  2. You verify your identity and complete the required ethics training.
  3. You work in the cloud Researcher Workbench. Data access is free; compute is paid, with starter credits provided.
- **Limitations:** Fitbit uses its own unpublished algorithms and there's no raw acceleration, so results are harder to compare with research-grade devices. Participants who share Fitbit data are a self-selected group. Medical records only cover care at participating health systems, so outcomes will be missed. Also, wear-time and data-quality rules work differently for long-term consumer data than for a fixed 7-day protocol.

## Smaller cohorts worth adding (useful for replication or pooling)

| Study | Wrist device and wear | Size | Outcomes | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Whitehall II** (UK civil servants) | GENEActiv, non-dominant wrist, about 9 days, 2012–13, raw data | About 4,000, aged 60–83 | Linked UK hospital records and death registry; dementia | Proposal to the study team at UCL, or through the Dementias Platform UK data portal |
| **MrOS Sleep** (older US men) | Wrist actigraph (Ambulatory Monitoring SleepWatch-O), about 5 days, 2003–05, activity counts | About 3,000 | Expert-reviewed deaths, fractures and cardiovascular events over long follow-up | Free registration on MrOS Online; actigraphy also on the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR) |
| **SOF** (older US women) | Wrist actigraph, about 3–5 days, 2002–04 | About 3,000 | Expert-reviewed deaths and fractures | Through the SOF/MrOS team at UCSF and NSRR |
| **MESA Sleep** (multi-ethnic US cohort) | Actiwatch Spectrum, wrist, 7 days, 2010–13 | About 2,200 | Expert-reviewed cardiovascular events and deaths | Actigraphy through NSRR (data use agreement, free); event data through NHLBI's BioLINCC repository or the MESA coordinating center |
| **China Kadoorie Biobank** | Axivity AX3, wrist, at the 2020–21 resurvey | About 20,000+ | Linked hospital insurance records and death registry | Through CKB's data access process; check whether the accelerometer data has been released yet |

MrOS, SOF and MESA are better suited to sleep and daily activity rhythms than to activity intensity. Their older devices record counts rather than raw signals.

## Why these studies may not match even though they're all wrist-worn
- **Which wrist:** UK Biobank used the dominant wrist. NHANES, Whitehall II and MESA used mostly the non-dominant wrist. The dominant wrist registers somewhat more movement, so check how much this shifts your cut-points.
- **Units:** UK Biobank and Whitehall II record raw g, usually summarised as ENMO. NHANES reports MIMS units. The older actigraphs record proprietary counts. To get comparable measures, reprocess the raw data with one pipeline where you can, such as GGIR or the Oxford `stepcount`/biobankAccelerometerAnalysis tools. Where only summaries exist, use rank-based or standardised exposures.
- **Not wrist-worn, despite being large:** the Women's Health Study, NHANES 2003–06, the German National Cohort (NAKO) and CARDIA used the hip, and HUNT4 used the thigh and back.

## What I'd suggest
1. Make UK Biobank your main analysis.
2. Replicate in NHANES 2011–14, which is quick and free.
3. Add Whitehall II, or MrOS/MESA if sleep is the focus, for checks in independent cohorts.

Treat All of Us as a separate consumer-device analysis rather than pooling it with the others. Start the UK Biobank and All of Us institutional paperwork early, because the agreements your university has to sign usually take the longest.

That gives roughly 8–10 years of follow-up after the wear week, so even fairly uncommon diseases have enough cases to study. This is the reference dataset most wrist-accelerometry outcome papers use.
- **Access:**
  1. Register yourself and your university on UK Biobank's Access Management System.
  2. Submit a research proposal. Approval usually takes weeks.
  3. Your institution signs a Material Transfer Agreement.
  4. Pay a tiered access fee, typically a few thousand pounds for three years, with reductions for students and early-career researchers.
- **Practical point:** analysis now happens only on UK Biobank's cloud platform (the Research Analysis Platform on DNAnexus). Data can't be downloaded, so budget for compute and storage, which matters if you reprocess the raw files. US universities apply routinely.

### 2. NHANES 2011–2014 (free, nationally representative US sample)
- **Device and wear:** ActiGraph GT3X+ on the **non-dominant wrist**, 7 days around the clock. About 7,000–9,000 adults have valid data. Minute-level summaries (in MIMS units) are public, and NCHS has also released the raw 80 Hz files.
- **Outcomes:** the public-use Linked Mortality Files connect participants to the National Death Index, including underlying cause of death. The most recent public follow-up I know of runs to the end of 2019, so check whether a newer one has been released. Medicare claims and the more detailed restricted mortality file are only available through an NCHS Research Data Center.
- **Access:** the public data has no application at all; you just download it. The Research Data Center route requires a proposal, a fee and work in a secure enclave.
- **Limitations:** mortality is the only outcome without the Research Data Center, follow-up is shorter, and the number of deaths is moderate. Use the survey weights. The older NHANES 2003–2006 accelerometer data was worn on the **hip**, so don't combine it with the wrist data.

### 3. All of Us Research Program (US, consumer trackers plus medical records)
- **Device and wear:** participants' own Fitbits (wrist-worn), plus devices the program has handed out. Tens of thousands of people have Fitbit data, often covering months to years. Measures include steps, heart rate, sleep stages and active minutes.
- **Outcomes:** electronic health records (diagnoses, procedures, labs) and surveys. Some mortality data exists. Check what the current release includes.
- **Access:**
  1. Your university signs a Data Use and Registration Agreement (many already have one).
  2. You verify your identity and complete the required ethics training.
  3. You work in the cloud Researcher Workbench. Data access is free; compute is paid, with starter credits provided.
- **Limitations:** Fitbit uses its own unpublished algorithms and there's no raw acceleration, so results are harder to compare with research-grade devices. Participants who share Fitbit data are a self-selected group. Medical records only cover care at participating health systems, so outcomes will be missed. Also, wear-time and data-quality rules work differently for long-term consumer data than for a fixed 7-day protocol.

## Smaller cohorts worth adding (useful for replication or pooling)

| Study | Wrist device and wear | Size | Outcomes | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Whitehall II** (UK civil servants) | GENEActiv, non-dominant wrist, about 9 days, 2012–13, raw data | About 4,000, aged 60–83 | Linked UK hospital records and death registry; dementia | Proposal to the study team at UCL, or through the Dementias Platform UK data portal |
| **MrOS Sleep** (older US men) | Wrist actigraph (Ambulatory Monitoring SleepWatch-O), about 5 days, 2003–05, activity counts | About 3,000 | Expert-reviewed deaths, fractures and cardiovascular events over long follow-up | Free registration on MrOS Online; actigraphy also on the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR) |
| **SOF** (older US women) | Wrist actigraph, about 3–5 days, 2002–04 | About 3,000 | Expert-reviewed deaths and fractures | Through the SOF/MrOS team at UCSF and NSRR |
| **MESA Sleep** (multi-ethnic US cohort) | Actiwatch Spectrum, wrist, 7 days, 2010–13 | About 2,200 | Expert-reviewed cardiovascular events and deaths | Actigraphy through NSRR (data use agreement, free); event data through NHLBI's BioLINCC repository or the MESA coordinating center |
| **China Kadoorie Biobank** | Axivity AX3, wrist, at the 2020–21 resurvey | About 20,000+ | Linked hospital insurance records and death registry | Through CKB's data access process; check whether the accelerometer data has been released yet |

MrOS, SOF and MESA are better suited to sleep and daily activity rhythms than to activity intensity. Their older devices record counts rather than raw signals.

## Why these studies may not match even though they're all wrist-worn
- **Which wrist:** UK Biobank used the dominant wrist. NHANES, Whitehall II and MESA used mostly the non-dominant wrist. The dominant wrist registers somewhat more movement, so check how much this shifts your cut-points.
- **Units:** UK Biobank and Whitehall II record raw g, usually summarised as ENMO. NHANES reports MIMS units. The older actigraphs record proprietary counts. To get comparable measures, reprocess the raw data with one pipeline where you can, such as GGIR or the Oxford `stepcount`/biobankAccelerometerAnalysis tools. Where only summaries exist, use rank-based or standardised exposures.
- **Not wrist-worn, despite being large:** the Women's Health Study, NHANES 2003–06, the German National Cohort (NAKO) and CARDIA used the hip, and HUNT4 used the thigh and back.

## What I'd suggest
1. Make UK Biobank your main analysis.
2. Replicate in NHANES 2011–14, which is quick and free.
3. Add Whitehall II, or MrOS/MESA if sleep is the focus, for checks in independent cohorts.

Treat All of Us as a separate consumer-device analysis rather than pooling it with the others. Start the UK Biobank and All of Us institutional paperwork early, because the agreements your university has to sign usually take the longest.

- **Which wrist:** UK Biobank used the dominant wrist. NHANES, Whitehall II and MESA used mostly the non-dominant wrist. The dominant wrist registers somewhat more movement, so check how much this shifts your cut-points.
- **Units:** UK Biobank and Whitehall II record raw g, usually summarised as ENMO. NHANES reports MIMS units. The older actigraphs record proprietary counts. Where only summaries exist, use rank-based or standardised exposures.
- **Not wrist-worn, despite being large:** the Women's Health Study, NHANES 2003–06, the German National Cohort (NAKO) and CARDIA used the hip, and HUNT4 used the thigh and back.

1. Make UK Biobank your main analysis.
2. Replicate in NHANES 2011–14, which is quick and free.
3. Add Whitehall II, or MrOS/MESA if sleep is the focus, for checks in independent cohorts.

Treat All of Us as a separate consumer-device analysis rather than pooling it with the others. Start the UK Biobank and All of Us institutional paperwork early, because the agreements your university has to sign usually take the longest.

For a US-based study of wrist accelerometry predicting later outcomes, the three main options are **UK Biobank** (largest, best outcome linkage), **NHANES 2011–2014** (free, US, linked to deaths) and **All of Us** (US, Fitbit plus medical records). After those come several smaller cohorts that are still useful. I wrote this from what I already know and didn't look anything up during this session. Treat fees, sample sizes and follow-up end dates as approximate, and check them on each study's site before you plan around them.

## Main options

### 1. UK Biobank accelerometer sub-study (best overall fit)
- **Device and wear:** Axivity AX3 on the **dominant wrist**, about 7 days of continuous wear, collected 2013–2015. Roughly 100,000 participants aged about 43–79. Raw 100 Hz data and processed summaries (activity, sleep and sedentary measures, ENMO) are both available. A few thousand participants also did repeat wears across seasons.
- **Outcomes:** linked hospital records for England, Scotland and Wales, national death and cancer registries, and GP records for part of the cohort. That gives roughly 8–10 years of follow-up after the wear week, so even fairly uncommon diseases have enough cases to study. This is the reference dataset most wrist-accelerometry outcome papers use.
- **Access:**
  1. Register yourself and your university on UK Biobank's Access Management System.
  2. Submit a research proposal. Approval usually takes weeks.
  3. Your institution signs a Material Transfer Agreement.
  4. Pay a tiered access fee, typically a few thousand pounds for three years, with reductions for students and early-career researchers.
- **Practical point:** analysis now happens only on UK Biobank's cloud platform (the Research Analysis Platform on DNAnexus). Data can't be downloaded, so budget for compute and storage, which matters if you reprocess the raw files. US universities apply routinely.

### 2. NHANES 2011–2014 (free, nationally representative US sample)
- **Device and wear:** ActiGraph GT3X+ on the **non-dominant wrist**, 7 days around the clock. About 7,000–9,000 adults have valid data. Minute-level summaries (in MIMS units) are public, and NCHS has also released the raw 80 Hz files.
- **Outcomes:** the public-use Linked Mortality Files connect participants to the National Death Index, including underlying cause of death. The most recent public follow-up I know of runs to the end of 2019, so check whether a newer one has been released. Medicare claims and the more detailed restricted mortality file are only available through an NCHS Research Data Center.
- **Access:** the public data has no application at all; you just download it. The Research Data Center route requires a proposal, a fee and work in a secure enclave.
- **Limitations:** mortality is the only outcome without the Research Data Center, follow-up is shorter, and the number of deaths is moderate. Use the survey weights. The older NHANES 2003–2006 accelerometer data was worn on the **hip**, so don't combine it with the wrist data.

### 3. All of Us Research Program (US, consumer trackers plus medical records)
- **Device and wear:** participants' own Fitbits (wrist-worn), plus devices the program has handed out. Tens of thousands of people have Fitbit data, often covering months to years. Measures include steps, heart rate, sleep stages and active minutes.
- **Outcomes:** electronic health records (diagnoses, procedures, labs) and surveys. Some mortality data exists. Check what the current release includes.
- **Access:**
  1. Your university signs a Data Use and Registration Agreement (many already have one).
  2. You verify your identity and complete the required ethics training.
  3. You work in the cloud Researcher Workbench. Data access is free; compute is paid, with starter credits provided.
- **Limitations:** Fitbit uses its own unpublished algorithms and there's no raw acceleration, so results are harder to compare with research-grade devices. Participants who share Fitbit data are a self-selected group. Medical records only cover care at participating health systems, so outcomes will be missed. Also, wear-time and data-quality rules work differently for long-term consumer data than for a fixed 7-day protocol.

## Main options

**1. UK Biobank, the largest option**
- **Data:** About 100,000 adults wore an Axivity AX3 on the dominant wrist for 7 days around 2013–2015. You get raw 100 Hz data plus derived summaries (ENMO, activity classes, sleep).
- **Outcomes:** Linked hospital admissions (HES and its Scottish and Welsh equivalents), cancer registry, death registry, and primary care records for part of the cohort. Follow-up now exceeds 10 years.
- **Access:**
  - Register as a researcher on the UK Biobank Access Management System, then submit a project application for health-related research.
  - After approval you sign a Material Transfer Agreement through your university and pay an access fee. It is a few thousand pounds, with discounts for students and some institutions; check the current rate.
  - Analysis now happens almost entirely on the cloud Research Analysis Platform (DNAnexus), not by download. You pay compute and storage costs there, which add up when processing raw accelerometer files.
  - US universities apply routinely. Expect weeks to a couple of months.

**2. NHANES 2011–2014, free and US-representative**
- **Data:** ActiGraph GT3X+ worn on the non-dominant wrist, 24 hours a day for 7 days. There are about 14,000 participants of all ages, roughly 9,000 adults. Public files contain minute-level MIMS summaries plus wear and sleep flags, and raw 80 Hz files have also been released.
- **Outcomes:**
  - The NCHS Public-Use Linked Mortality Files (National Death Index) give vital status and broad cause of death. Current follow-up runs through 2019.
  - The restricted mortality files, plus Medicare (CMS) linkage, are available only through an NCHS/CDC Research Data Center.
- **Access:**
  - The public data and mortality files are free downloads with no application.
  - The restricted data require an RDC proposal and, usually, work in a secure enclave. They allow finer cause of death, exact dates, and claims data that approximate disease incidence.
- **Caution:** NHANES 2003–2006 used hip-worn devices, so only the 2011–2014 cycles fit your wrist requirement.

**3. All of Us Research Program, consumer trackers linked to medical records**
- **Data:** Fitbit data from participants' own devices: steps, heart rate, sleep stages and activity minutes. Recent releases cover tens of thousands of participants, often with months to years of data, linked to EHR diagnoses, procedures, labs and some death data.
- **Access:**
  - Your institution signs a Data Use and Registration Agreement; most large US universities already have.
  - You register with an identity check and complete responsible-conduct training.
  - The Registered Tier is available quickly. The Controlled Tier is usually needed for this kind of work and requires extra training.
  - All analysis happens on the cloud Researcher Workbench. New users get starter credits, then pay compute costs. There is no project-level scientific review, so access is fast, often days.
- **Caveats for comparability:**
  - You get proprietary Fitbit summaries, not raw accelerometry, so they don't map directly onto ENMO or MIMS.
  - Participants are self-selected device owners.
  - Wear patterns vary a lot between people.
  - Outcomes depend on how complete each person's EHR is.

## Smaller cohorts with stronger outcome adjudication

| Cohort | Wrist device and size | Outcomes | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Whitehall II** (UK civil servants) | GENEActiv, non-dominant wrist, 9 days, about 4,000 adults (2012–13) | NHS hospital records, mortality, dementia | Proposal to the Whitehall II team at UCL; reviewed, sometimes with collaboration expected |
| **MrOS Sleep** (older US men) | Wrist actigraph, about 5 days, about 3,000 men | Adjudicated mortality, CVD, fractures | Wrist actigraphy via the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR, sleepdata.org) under a short DUA; extra follow-up outcomes from the MrOS coordinating center |
| **SOF** (older US women) | Wrist actigraph, about 3 days, about 3,000 women | Mortality, fractures, cognitive decline | NSRR / SOF Online |
| **MESA Sleep** | Actiwatch Spectrum, wrist, 7 days, about 2,000 adults | Adjudicated CVD events, mortality | Actigraphy via NSRR; events via BioLINCC or the MESA coordinating center, which require IRB approval and a DUA |
| **HCHS/SOL Sueño** | Actiwatch, wrist, about 2,000 Hispanic/Latino adults | Ongoing cohort follow-up | NSRR plus the HCHS/SOL coordinating center |
| **Rotterdam Study** | Wrist actigraphy (GENEActiv in later rounds), a few thousand adults | GP records, hospital records, mortality | Collaboration with Erasmus MC, not an open application |
| **China Kadoorie Biobank** | Axivity on the wrist in a recent resurvey subsample of about 20,000 or more | Hospital insurance and death registry linkage | CKB data access portal. Check whether the accelerometer data have been released yet; my information may be out of date |

The MrOS, SOF and MESA devices are sleep-focused actigraphs that record proprietary counts. They work well for sleep and rest-activity rhythms, but are harder to harmonize with raw-data metrics.

## Exclusions (not wrist-worn)

- **Hip:** Women's Health Study, OPACH, Tromsø, NAKO, and NHANES 2003–06.
- **Thigh or back:** HUNT and the 1970 British Cohort Study.
- **Chest:** Fenland.

## Practical suggestions

- **Pairing:** A common design is UK Biobank for discovery and NHANES 2011–14 for US replication. Both are 24-hour wrist protocols with raw data available. They differ in device (Axivity vs ActiGraph), wrist (dominant vs non-dominant) and metric (ENMO vs MIMS). Processing raw data from both with the same pipeline, such as GGIR or the Oxford `stepcount`/`biobankAccelerometerAnalysis` tools, improves comparability.
- **Order of applications:** Start with NHANES public data and NSRR, which take days. Run UK Biobank and All of Us applications in parallel. File an RDC proposal only if you need restricted NHANES mortality or Medicare data.
- **Ethics:** Your university IRB will usually classify secondary analysis of these de-identified data as exempt or not human-subjects research. Some providers, such as NSRR and BioLINCC, still require that determination letter.

Fees, sample counts and follow-up dates change between releases, so check each provider's current access pages before budgeting.

- **Data:** Fitbit data from participants' own devices: steps, heart rate, sleep stages and activity minutes. Recent releases cover tens of thousands of participants, often with months to years of data, linked to EHR diagnoses, procedures, labs and some death data.
- **Access:**
  - Your institution signs a Data Use and Registration Agreement; most large US universities already have.
  - You register with an identity check and complete responsible-conduct training.
  - The Registered Tier is available quickly. The Controlled Tier is usually needed for this kind of work and requires extra training.
  - All analysis happens on the cloud Researcher Workbench. New users get starter credits, then pay compute costs. There is no project-level scientific review, so access is fast, often days.
- **Caveats for comparability:**
  - You get proprietary Fitbit summaries, not raw accelerometry, so they don't map directly onto ENMO or MIMS.
  - Participants are self-selected device owners.
  - Wear patterns vary a lot between people.
  - Outcomes depend on how complete each person's EHR is.

## Smaller cohorts with stronger outcome adjudication

| Cohort | Wrist device and size | Outcomes | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Whitehall II** (UK civil servants) | GENEActiv, non-dominant wrist, 9 days, about 4,000 adults (2012–13) | NHS hospital records, mortality, dementia | Proposal to the Whitehall II team at UCL; reviewed, sometimes with collaboration expected |
| **MrOS Sleep** (older US men) | Wrist actigraph, about 5 days, about 3,000 men | Adjudicated mortality, CVD, fractures | Wrist actigraphy via the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR, sleepdata.org) under a short DUA; extra follow-up outcomes from the MrOS coordinating center |
| **SOF** (older US women) | Wrist actigraph, about 3 days, about 3,000 women | Mortality, fractures, cognitive decline | NSRR / SOF Online |
| **MESA Sleep** | Actiwatch Spectrum, wrist, 7 days, about 2,000 adults | Adjudicated CVD events, mortality | Actigraphy via NSRR; events via BioLINCC or the MESA coordinating center, which require IRB approval and a DUA |
| **HCHS/SOL Sueño** | Actiwatch, wrist, about 2,000 Hispanic/Latino adults | Ongoing cohort follow-up | NSRR plus the HCHS/SOL coordinating center |
| **Rotterdam Study** | Wrist actigraphy (GENEActiv in later rounds), a few thousand adults | GP records, hospital records, mortality | Collaboration with Erasmus MC, not an open application |
| **China Kadoorie Biobank** | Axivity on the wrist in a recent resurvey subsample of about 20,000 or more | Hospital insurance and death registry linkage | CKB data access portal. Check whether the accelerometer data have been released yet; my information may be out of date |

The MrOS, SOF and MESA devices are sleep-focused actigraphs that record proprietary counts. They work well for sleep and rest-activity rhythms, but are harder to harmonize with raw-data metrics.

## Exclusions (not wrist-worn)

- **Hip:** Women's Health Study, OPACH, Tromsø, NAKO, and NHANES 2003–06.
- **Thigh or back:** HUNT and the 1970 British Cohort Study.
- **Chest:** Fenland.

## Practical suggestions

- **Pairing:** A common design is UK Biobank for discovery and NHANES 2011–14 for US replication. Both are 24-hour wrist protocols with raw data available. They differ in device (Axivity vs ActiGraph), wrist (dominant vs non-dominant) and metric (ENMO vs MIMS). Processing raw data from both with the same pipeline, such as GGIR or the Oxford `stepcount`/`biobankAccelerometerAnalysis` tools, improves comparability.
- **Order of applications:** Start with NHANES public data and NSRR, which take days. Run UK Biobank and All of Us applications in parallel. File an RDC proposal only if you need restricted NHANES mortality or Medicare data.
- **Ethics:** Your university IRB will usually classify secondary analysis of these de-identified data as exempt or not human-subjects research. Some providers, such as NSRR and BioLINCC, still require that determination letter.

Fees, sample counts and follow-up dates change between releases, so check each provider's current access pages before budgeting.

| **MrOS / SOF** | Wrist actigraphs (older devices) | ~3,000 men / ~3,000 women | 3–5 days | Death, fractures, other events | NSRR or the study portals |

### 1. UK Biobank (your main dataset)
- **Why:** It is the largest wrist study with raw data, and most published wrist-based work on activity, sleep and outcomes uses it. That makes comparing your results with other studies easy.
- **Data:** You get raw files plus derived variables: ENMO acceleration, machine-learned activity and sleep classes, and step counts from the Oxford group's models. Outcomes come through linked hospital records, death and cancer registries. Primary care records cover about 45% of participants.
- **Caveats:** Participants are healthier than the general population and mostly white British. The device was worn on the dominant wrist, while NHANES and Whitehall II used the non-dominant wrist. Activity was measured about 5 years after baseline.
- **Access:**
  1. Register on the Access Management System. Your university and you as a researcher both need to be approved, which usually takes days to a couple of weeks.
  2. Submit a short proposal. Approval usually takes a few weeks.
  3. Sign the Material Transfer Agreement, which your institution signs.
  4. Pay the access fee. It is tiered, roughly several thousand pounds for a 3-year project; check the current rates.
- **Analysis environment:** Since 2024, analysis happens only on the cloud Research Analysis Platform (DNAnexus). You can't download data, and you pay compute and storage costs, which add up when processing raw accelerometer files. Separate ethics approval usually isn't needed, because UK Biobank has its own ethics approval, but check with your IRB.

### 2. NHANES 2011–2014 (easiest to get, and US-representative)
- **Data:** Wrist-worn, 24-hour wear for 7 days. Activity is released as MIMS units at minute, hour and day level, with flags for wear, sleep and non-wear. Mortality comes from the public NCHS Linked Mortality File, currently through Dec 31, 2019.
- **Access:** Download it from the CDC website now, no application needed. The restricted mortality file has the exact date of death and more detail; it requires an NCHS Research Data Center proposal, which takes months and has fees.
- **Caveats:** Death is the only outcome; there are no hospital records in the public files. The number of deaths is modest, about 1,000 or fewer in adults depending on the subset. Raw-data processing pipelines like GGIR need to be adapted to MIMS units. The 2003–2006 NHANES waves used a hip-worn device, so leave them out.

### 3. All of Us Research Program
- **Data:** Fitbit records of steps, heart rate, sleep stages and activity minutes, linked to electronic health records. Some participants have years of data, which allows long-term studies of habitual behavior.
- **Caveats:** These are consumer devices and only processed summaries are available, not raw acceleration, so results aren't directly comparable with research-grade studies. People who own Fitbits are a selected group. Outcomes depend on what the health records capture.
- **Access:**
  1. Your university must sign a Data Use and Registration Agreement; many US universities already have.
  2. You verify your identity, complete research ethics training and sign the code of conduct.
  3. Fitbit data is in the Registered Tier. Some detailed health record fields and dates are in the Controlled Tier, which requires extra training.
- **Analysis environment:** Free to use, but analysis happens on the cloud Researcher Workbench with initial credits, then you pay for compute. No IRB review is usually needed, and you must follow their publication and data-display rules.

### 4. Whitehall II (UK civil servants)
- **Data:** About 4,000 people wore GENEActiv devices on the wrist for 9 days in 2012–13. Raw data is available, with about a decade of linked hospital, death and dementia records. It is widely used for sleep, physical activity and dementia studies.
- **Access:** Submit a data-sharing proposal to the Whitehall II team at UCL. Data may come through the Dementias Platform UK portal. Expect a few months and a data-sharing agreement. The cohort is older and mostly male, with office-worker backgrounds.

### 5. Sleep-focused US cohorts via the National Sleep Research Resource (sleepdata.org)
- **MESA Sleep:** Wrist actigraphy plus sleep studies in a multi-ethnic sample. The NSRR provides the actigraphy. Adjudicated heart disease events and deaths may need a separate MESA paper proposal or the NHLBI biobank, BioLINCC.
- **MrOS and SOF:** Older men and women, with death and fracture follow-up. The devices are older, with limited activity information, so these are mainly useful for sleep and rest-activity rhythms.
- **Access:** NSRR asks for an online data access request, a data use agreement signed by your institution, and usually documentation of IRB approval or exemption. It is free and typically takes weeks.

### Others to watch or rule out
- **China Kadoorie Biobank:** About 20,000+ participants wore Axivity devices on the wrist in a recent resurvey, with linked hospital and death records. Check whether the accelerometer data has been released yet through its data access process.
- **Rotterdam Study and Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging:** Both have wrist GENEActiv data but smaller samples, and access requires collaborating with the study team.
- **Studies that don't fit:** Women's Health Study and OPACH (hip), NHANES 2003–06 (hip), CARDIA and Framingham (hip), HUNT4 (thigh and back) and the German National Cohort, NAKO (hip).

## Tips for comparability
- **Wrist side:** Record which wrist was used. UK Biobank used the dominant wrist; NHANES and Whitehall II used the non-dominant wrist. This shifts activity intensity estimates somewhat.
- **Processing:** Where you have raw data (UK Biobank, Whitehall II), process it with standard open tools such as GGIR or the Oxford `stepcount` and `asleep` models, and report ENMO or MIMS so other researchers can compare. Results based on MIMS and ENMO need to be harmonized before you pool or compare them.
- **Order of access:** A practical sequence is NHANES first, since you can download it today and use it for US mortality, then UK Biobank as the main analysis, then Whitehall II or All of Us for replication.

The fees, follow-up dates and sample sizes above are from memory. Check them on each program's website before you put them in a grant or IRB application.
